Enhanced Conductivity and CO <sub>2</sub> Activation in Li-Doped 2D Polyaramid: A DFT Study on the Electronic Structure and Catalytic Performance
Exploring the Electronic Nature of Spinel Oxides: A Review of Their Electron Interactions and Prospects
abstract: This review discusses the multifaceted electronic properties of spinel oxides with a particular focus on Lithium Vanadate (LiV2O4), Lithium Titanate (LiTi2O4), and Magnesium Titanate (MgTi2O4). We selected LiTi2O4, LiV2O4, and MgTi2O4 because they serve as quintessential examples of spinel oxides' diverse and intriguing electronic phenomena. LiV2O4 heavy fermion behaviour challenges traditional theories in d-electron systems, LiTi2O4 being the first oxide superconductor provides critical insights into unconventional superconductivity driven by strong electron-phonon interactions, and MgTi2O4 pronounced orbital ordering and metalinsulator transition offers a clear model for exploring electron-lattice coupling. This shows how the inherent structural versatility of the spinel lattice, characterised by its cubic close-packed oxygen network and variable cation distributions, enables a rich interplay of electron-electron correlations, electron-lattice coupling, and orbital degrees of freedom. In LiV2O4, the combination of mixed-valence vanadium ions and a geometrically frustrated pyrochlore lattice gives rise to heavy fermion behaviour, whereas LiTi2O4 exhibits unconventional superconductivity driven by a high density of states at the Fermi level and strong electronphonon interactions. MgTi2O4 undergoes a pronounced metal-insulator transition, where orbital ordering triggers a Peierls-like distortion that stabilises a low-temperature insulating state through Ti-Ti dimerization. How the composition of these compounds affects their properties, based on both theoretical research and experimental findings, is illustrated by this review. It illustrates the promise of Spinels in practical technologies such as energy storage, electrocatalysis, and high-temperature lubrication.

title: Advances in Mg–Fe Layered Double Hydroxides: Sustainable Water Treatment & Circular Economy Integration
abstract: Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are a promising group of materials for sustainable water treatment. They have adjustable structures, can exchange ions, and are safe for the environment. Among these, magnesium-iron (Mg-Fe) LDHs stand out because they are readily available, low in toxicity, and very effective at removing anions. This review looks at recent advancements in Mg-Fe LDHs, focusing on their potential in circular economy models. These materials can successfully eliminate contaminants such as phosphates, nitrates, fluoride, arsenate, humic acid, heavy metals, dyes, and pharmaceuticals through ion exchange, surface complexation, precipitation, and structural memory effects. Changes like adding biochar, creating magnetic hybrids, and activating catalysts further improve contaminant removal and recyclability. Spent Mg-Fe LDHs can also be reused as slow-release fertilizers or catalysts, promoting the idea of using waste as a resource. Studies on thermodynamics and kinetics indicate that adsorption usually follows spontaneous, pseudo-second-order behavior with Langmuir-type isotherms. The ability to regenerate and reuse these LDHs strengthens their role in adsorption-based cleanup and advanced oxidation methods. In the circular economy model, Mg-Fe LDHs help shift from traditional pollutant removal to efficiently recovering resources and managing wastewater. This review covers synthesis methods, adsorption mechanisms, regeneration behavior, and practical applications, highlighting key research gaps for scaling up. Future research should aim at integrating renewable energy, using green synthesis techniques, and exploring industrial symbiosis to improve the environmental performance and cost-effectiveness of Mg-Fe LDH-based water treatment systems.

title: Design principles for adaptive and evolving engineered living materials
3D Outcrop-Based Carbonate Seismic Property Model: A Medium to Model the Impact of Meter-Scale Near-Surface Geological Heterogeneity on Seismic Data
abstract: The published dataset is a high-resolution 3D seismic property model. The model explicitly captures meter-scale facies heterogeneity representing the typical near-surface geology of desert carbonate strata. The model is provided in 32-bit SEG-Y format, ready for direct use in seismic modeling and simulation software. The model dimensions are ~4 km x 4 km x 155 deep, with a fine grid resolution of 3 m x 3 m x 0.3 m (X,Y,Z).The model includes VP (m/s), VS (m/s), and density (g/cc). The model is constructed based on extensive Late Jurassic outcrop and near-surface core data. This model accurately replicates complex facies architecture and petrophysical variations observed in the shallow subsurface of the Arabian Desert. This resource is essential for forward modeling studies and testing advanced acquisition/processing methods designed to mitigate seismic data degradation caused by strong wavefield scattering from shallow geological heterogeneities.

Timing of Deformation in the Provence Fold-and-Thrust Belt (SE France) as Constrained by U-Pb Calcite Geochronology
abstract: A combination of fault and fracture analyses, paleostress reconstructions from calcite twins, and U-Pb dating of syn-kinematic calcite mineralization provides new insights into the Cretaceous–Tertiary tectonic evolution of the Provence fold-and-thrust belt. This approach helped unravel 90 million years of polyphase deformation in this belt, which represents the eastward continuation of the northern Pyrenees. Focusing on three main targets along an NNE-SSW transect oriented roughly parallel to the regional Pyrenean shortening (the southernmost Nerthe range, the Bimont Lake area, and the northern Rians syncline), we date a wide range of scales and natures of deformation structures such as stylolites, veins, mesoscale faults, and major thrust fault zones. The reconstructed long-lasting tectonic history includes (1) the Durancian uplift and related NNE-SSW extension (~110 to 90 Ma); (2) the ~N-S Pyrenean compression related to the convergence then collision between Eurasia and Iberia and the Corsica–Sardinia block (~80 to 34 Ma); the Oligocene E-W to WNW-ESE extension related to the West European Cenozoic Rift System (ECRIS) and the Oligo–Miocene NW-SE to NNW-SSE extension related to the Liguro-Provençal Rifting (LPR); and a middle-late (?) N-S to NW-SE Alpine compression. We show that the Pyrenean shortening in Provence occurred during two main phases, 81–69 Ma and 59–34 Ma, coeval with the inversion of the pre-Pyrenean rift and the main Pyrenean collision, separated by a tectonic quiescence as described in the Pyrenees. Together with the published literature, our U-Pb ages also support the overall northward (forelandward) in sequence propagation of Pyrenean shortening across Provence. Our U-Pb results further allow us to refine the interpretation of local and regional fracture sets and reveal unsuspected polyphase development of fractures sharing a common strike. Beyond regional implications, our study shows that sampling structures of various natures and scales for U-Pb geochronology is probably the most efficient strategy to encompass the entire time interval of deformation in fold-and-thrust belts.

title: Age-model codes and paleoearthquake ages for the Frazier Mountain, Pallett Creek, and Wrightwood paleoseismic sites along the Southern San Andreas Fault, California
abstract: These datasets provide age-model codes and resultant paleoearthquake age distributions for three paleoseismic sites along the southern San Andreas Fault. The code format is compatible with the age-model program OxCal (Bronk Ramsey 2009) which calibrates radiocarbon dates to calendar years and uses stratigraphic relationships among radiocarbon samples and sedimentary units to compute paleoearthquake ages. Earthquake age distributions are provided as CSV files. The source data were developed as part of primary investigations into the timing of past earthquakes at each site. This data release provides necessary stratigraphic context to reconstruct the earthquake ages in OxCal. Users are encouraged to access the original reports for context on the radiocarbon samples, stratigraphy, earthquake evidence and quality, and depositional environment at each site.

abstract: Seismic data recorded in association with the U.S. NSF-funded West Greenland Moulins project, on the Greenland Ice Sheet, within Sermeq Avannarleq (NSF Awards 1604022 and 1603835). The purpose of the project was to better understand the role of water flowing into moulins on the ice sheet surface in governing the motion of the Greenland Ice Sheet. In 2008, 8 seismometers were maintained within the ice sheet ablation area between April and October in order to track glaciohydraulic tremor produced by subglacial water flow, as well as seismic signals associated with the response of the ice sheet to that water flow. Our network consisted of two types of stations: 1) Geobit SRi32L digitizers connected to C100 seismometers with nominally flat frequency response between 10 s and 98 Hz, and 2) Nanometrics Centaur digitizers connected to Trillium Compact Posthole seismometers, with 20 s corner period. Sensors were installed below the snow-ice interface, 1.2 - 2.5 m deep in augered holes and connected to lead acid batteries powered by solar panels.

title: Revised History of Pleistocene Vertical Motions in NE Sicily and Southern Calabria, Italy, from 40Ar/39Ar Dating and Fault Zone Morphology
abstract: Long-term rates of crustal uplift in southern Calabria and NE Sicily are incompletely understood due to limited information about the age of marine terraces at 1.0–1.3 km above sea level (asl). This study provides a new constraint on high-elevation terrace ages through integrated analysis of geochronology, stratigraphy, shoreline modeling, and fault-zone morphology. 40Ar/39Ar step-heating experiments on glass from a tuff in marine claystone of the Argille di Spadafora, NE Sicily, yield reproducible age spectra with a mean age of 0.481 ± 0.019 Ma (± 2σ). The Argille di Spadafora and equivalent marl in southern Calabria are overlain by Pleistocene marine terrace deposits, indicating the terraces are younger than 0.50 Ma. Paleoshoreline modeling at Campo Piale, southern Calabria, suggests an age of 525–590 ka for a terrace at 600–630 m asl: this is an overestimate because it assumes no fault offsets, tilting or structural warping despite geomorphic evidence for these processes. We correlate the 630-m terrace to the marine terrace at 1.0–1.3 km asl based on recognition of a relay ramp between the Cittanova and Sant’Eufemia faults, and geomorphic evidence for fault offset of the terrace. We conclude that marine terraces up to 1.0–1.3 km asl are all &lt; 0.50 Ma, roughly half the widely cited estimate of 1.0 ± 0.2 Ma. The revised age suggests an average uplift rate of &gt; 2.5 mm/y for the highest terrace, and variable throw rates up to 1.0 mm/y on normal faults that cut the terraces.

title: Large-scale flow toward low-velocity anomalies reconciles seismic and geodynamic constraints in the deepest mantle beneath Alaska
abstract: Deep mantle downwellings are typically located away from the two Large Low-Velocity Provinces (LLVPs) in Earth's mantle. Geodynamic models based on global seismic tomography generally predict that convective flow at the core-mantle boundary (CMB) spreads laterally away from downwelling regions and towards LLVPs. While this offers a framework for understanding large-scale deformation in the lowermost mantle, it has yet to be confirmed by seismic constraints. This study investigates seismic anisotropy and wave reflections in the deepest mantle beneath Alaska, linking a known reflector to the inferred deformation. To capture large-scale deformation, the analysis utilizes waves with long raypaths through the deepest mantle. Mantle shear direction is then determined using global wavefield simulations that incorporate mineral physics constraints. The inferred North-South shear direction agrees with findings for an adjacent region beneath the northeastern Pacific Ocean, together forming a continuous ~3000 km x 3000 km region where the inferred southward shear aligns with geodynamic model predictions. These results support a first-order framework of lowermost mantle deformation driven by flow away from downwellings and toward LLVPs.

Black Crust Versus Substrate on Historic Stone: A brief pXRF Study at Golia Monastery (Iași, Romania)
abstract: Black crusts are a recurrent alteration feature on historic masonry, particularly in urban environments affected by traffic emissions and atmospheric pollutants. This study investigates the chemical contrast between a dark black-crust band and the underlying stone substrate on the western enclosure wall of Golia Monastery (Iași, Romania), using portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) as a non-invasive analytical tool. Fourteen in-situ measurements were performed on a single buttress to quantify key elements (S, Cl, Ca, Ti, Fe, Cu, Zn) and to derive diagnostic ratios (S/Ca, Cl/Ca, Cu/Ti, Zn/Ti, Fe/Ti) together with median-based enrichment factors. The results show that the wall is built of calcareous sandstone, while the black crust represents a composite deposit formed by gypsum crystallization within a matrix of siliciclastic dust and carbonate particles. Among all indicators, S/Ca exhibits the clearest contrast: the median S/Ca ratio in the crust (~0.054) is approximately twice that of the substrate (~0.025), yielding an enrichment factor EF(S/Ca) ≈ 2.1 and confirming sulfate enrichment and gypsum development on the exposed band. By contrast, Cl/Ca remains low in both zones, and Ti-normalized metal ratios (Cu/Ti, Zn/Ti, Fe/Ti) are strongly constrained by detection limits, preventing robust interpretation in terms of traffic-derived particulates. Small but measurable amounts of P suggest a certain degree of bioreceptivity of the crust surface, although this hypothesis requires microanalytical confirmation. From a Conservation Science perspective, the study demonstrates that pXRF-based ratio analysis can rapidly document sulfate-enriched black crusts on heritage stonework while also highlighting the limitations of trace-metal indicators in small in situ datasets and the need for combined chemical, microstructural, and biological approaches.

Mineral chemistry and petrological modelling results of melting experiments of a CM carbonaceous chondrite
abstract: This dataset documents the major- and trace-element characteristics of experimental products generated from high-pressure melting experiments on the CM2 chondrite MCY 12002. The data were produced to investigate the differentiation behaviour of volatile-rich carbonaceous chondrite material and to constrain the formation of sulphide-, metal-, and silicate-rich melts under controlled redox and thermal conditions. The dataset includes (i) electron microprobe (EMPA) major-element compositions of olivine, low- and high-Ca pyroxene, quenched silicate melt, spinel, FeNi metal and S-rich phase; (ii) LA-ICP-MS trace-element maps and spot analyses of olivine phenocrysts and silicate melt pools; and (iii) mass-balance models constraining melt-silicates relationships. Together, these data provide a comprehensive geochemical characterisation of the run products and allow reproducibility of the petrological interpretations.

title: Provenance Modelling of Fossil Dinosaur Bones Using Geochemistry and Machine Learning: Source Data
abstract: The data presented here support the research paper “Provenance Modelling of Fossil Dinosaur Bones Using Geochemistry and Machine Learning”, intended for a submission to "Palaeoworld". The dataset contains trace elements concentrations from fossil dinosaur bones from the Upper Cretaceous Nemegt and Djadokhta formations. For the analytical purposes, the dataset was divided into two subsets: the first one consisting of long bones (tibiae, femora, radii and humeri) and the other including trabecular bones (ribs and vertebrae) and metatarsals. Locality labels were used to train and evaluate several machine learning classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) to assess the potential of bone geochemistry for provenance prediction. Feature selection was conducted on the best-performing models to identify the elements contributing the most to the model performance. These results were compared with those obtained using Linear Discriminant Analysis. The data are provided in CSV format in the “Data” folder. The folder “Plots and figures” contains the figures used in the manuscript, including the plots. The folder “Supplementary files” contains additional files. These files are: - interactive HTML plot ("Element profiles.html") showing the all the concentration profiles across each analysed sample, including the ones measured along several profiles - concentration profiles presented in a PDF file ("All profiles.pdf") - XLSX file with the statistical summary of the data ("Data description WK.xlsx") - LDA scalings in CSV file ("LDA scalings.csv") - The tables comparing predictions and performance of the algorithms using test part of each subset ("Predictions and accuracy.xlsx") Besides that, the Jupyter Notebook with data analysis is also provided ("Bones from Gobi - loc prediction.ipynb").

Why the Earth's crust moves: thermodynamics, Isostasy and the enabling role of liquid water
abstract: It is undisputed that the Earth's surface moves both horizontally and vertically (e.g. mountain formation). The currently dominant theory of plate tectonics argues that a combination of seafloor spreading (Hess 1962), slab pull (Forsyth and Uyeda, 1975) and convection currents (Ampferer, 1906) in the planet's interior causes the Earth's crust to move (Meschede et al., 2022). The predictive power of the plate tectonics theory regarding plate motions appears convincing (see Fossen and Teysier (2025) for an overview) and was so decisive that other theories (incl. their derivations; see Meschede et al. (2022) for an overview) have already been rejected, incl. the theories of geological thermal cycles (Joly, 1925; Holmes, 1929, 1930), degassing (Barth, 1952), undation (van Bemmelen, 1933), oscillation (Haarmann, 1930), expansion (Carey, 1975), contraction (Dana, 1873), continental drift (Wegener, 1912, 1915) – the predecessor of the current plate tectonics theory – or the flowing hypothesis (Gutenberg, 1927). However, the precise mechanisms driving plate tectonics remain elusive due to a convergence of modelling complexity, observational constraints and theoretical uncertainty. The inability to directly measure deep Earth forces or accurately simulate key processes prevents definitive validation. Models are hampered by poorly constrained physical parameters, and geophysical imaging provides only indirect proxies for the dynamic forces at play. The same applies to the subduction hypothesis and the necessary recycling of the crust in the form of remelting. Without subduction, the plate tectonic model cannot work. However, it remains unclear how the process of subduction was supposed to have started in the first place, and this is a question that is still being debated. The main challenge is to identify a mechanism by which a strong lithosphere might break in the absence of plate tectonics-related weak zones and slab driving forces (Lu et al., 2021). It is not the purpose of this paper to discuss the weaknesses of the plate tectonic theory or other already rejected approaches in detail. It would simply go beyond the scope of this paper. However, we believe that the open questions and uncertainties about the driving forces of plate tectonics leave room for an alternative explanation. We therefore want to focus in this paper on a completely different, new explanatory approach. We will describe a mechanism that can be used to explain both horizontal and vertical movements as well as adjustment processes of a planet’s crust. In our view, our approach provides a coherent model that addresses causes and consequences, and we also claim that the predictions of our model are perfectly in line with the actual movements of the Earth's crust as measured by the GNSS Time Series provided by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (Heflin et al., 2020). Among other things, our new theory can easily answer four key questions about the movement of the planetary crust. The first two are directly derived from the mentioned GNSS observations. First, why is there not a single mountain range on Earth where adjacent crustal fragments are moving towards each other? How can mountains still fold? Second, why are the only zones where crustal fragments move directly towards each other some transition zones between high plateaus of continents (and islands) and deep basins of oceans (and seas)? Third, why are crustal movements so intense on Earth in particular, while they are often not observable on other planets? Finally, why do earthquakes occur repeatedly even within large continents far away from known fault zones, whereas this is rarely the case in the interior of ocean floor fragments (with the exception of their edges)? As novel as our approach may be, it does not require any new physical, chemical or other findings or assumptions about processes in the Earth’s interior that cannot be directly observed or measured. Only the GNSS dataset on the movement directions of the Earth's crust (Heflin et al., 2020), which helped us to identify the mechanism, can be described as new, as it was not available at the time the plate tectonics theory was first developed. The described mechanism is the result of analyzing this relatively new dataset and is based solely on fundamental scientific principles that are beyond dispute. We refer to the laws of thermodynamics, Archimedes' principle of buoyancy in liquids, and material properties such as thermal conductivity, density, and breaking and tensile strength. Everything else is just a matter of logical deduction. Unlike the explanatory approaches we are familiar with, however, the root cause here is not the horizontal movements of the Earth's crust, which subsequently might cause vertical movements (such as the folding of the crust during mountain formation). Based on the laws of thermodynamics, we will describe how differences in the average thermal conductivity of the regionally predominant rock types lead to different rates of crustal thickening due to the continuous cooling of the planet (section 6). This subsequently necessitates ongoing adjustments to new isostatic equilibria in the form of (relative) vertical uplift and subsidence movements of the crust (see section 2). Each upward and downward movement not only deforms the rigid crust, but also, due to the spherical shape of the planet, is accompanied by an (layer-by-layer) enlargement of the surface of the crust (see section 3). Due to its severely limited elasticity and deformability, the existing crust cannot simply adapt to the new conditions like a balloon, for example, but must inevitably tear, break, or move horizontally in order to resolve the horizontal tension caused by the vertical movements. The cavities caused by fractures and cracks subsequently lead to changes in the average density of the crust (per base area) and cause further disruptions in the isostatic equilibrium, the consequences of which have a similar effect (see sections 4 and 5). On planet Earth, this mechanism is particularly strong compared to other celestial bodies, as there are significant amounts of liquid water on the surface. Due to its significantly lower thermal conductivity compared to rocks, liquid water acts as an additional strongly heat-insulating layer and delays the cooling of the planet (and thus also the further growth of the crust's thickness), especially in areas where it collects in large quantities. However, since these deep basins of today's oceans and seas have only formed due to the low thermal conductivity of the rock types prevailing there, the water further exacerbates the global differences in the crust’s thickness growth. The basins of the oceans are becoming deeper, while the high plateaus of the continents are rising ever higher. The liquid water acts as a catalyst, further amplifying the resulting effects of regional differences in the rate of crustal thickening (see sections 7 and 8).

title: Roman Forts in the Northern Black Sea Area Through the Lens of Drone‐Based Magnetometry
abstract: ABSTRACT Drone‐based magnetometry has demonstrated high effectiveness in verifying satellite observations and detecting new archaeological features. In this study, we evaluate its application for archaeological prospection in the Northern Black Sea region, focusing on the previously documented Roman fort Kamianka V and one newly identified fort. DJI Agras T30 drones equipped with SENSYS MagDrone R3 magnetometers were used to survey areas of 14.0 and 1.6 ha on two sites. The magnetometer was suspended on a 2.0‐m extension boom to minimize interference from the drone's electronics and to maintain the sensors' altitude of 1.0 m above the ground. The achieved survey accuracy, estimated as ±1.05 nT, enabled reliable detection of ditch structures—key elements of Roman fortifications—based on anomalies ranging from 1 to 12 nT. Comparison with the ground‐based magnetometer survey demonstrates a close correspondence in the observed magnetic patterns. The layout of the Kamianka V fort, which is atypical for Roman military architecture, has been confirmed—featuring two internal forts enclosed within a single outer defensive system. The New fort was identified as a square‐shaped positive magnetic anomaly consistent with a Roman‐period enclosure. The study demonstrates the strong potential of drone‐based magnetometry for large‐area, high‐resolution archaeological mapping in the steppe environment, including the detection of subtle earthen structures often obscured by intensive agricultural land use. These findings contribute to ongoing research on Roman military presence in the Northern Black Sea region and illustrate how drone‐based geophysical solutions can expand the spatial and historical understanding of frontier systems.

title: Invisible water in subducted crust: Lawsonite velocity anomalies under mantle conditions
abstract: Subduction zones transport significant amounts of water into Earth’s mantle, primarily through hydrous minerals such as lawsonite. However, the seismic detectability of lawsonite-bearing oceanic crust at mantle depths remains uncertain. To address this issue, we measured sound velocities of lawsonite up to 7.4 GPa and 600 °C. Both P- and S-wave velocities exhibited unexpected increases with temperature under high-pressure conditions. Our result suggest that hydrous oceanic crust exhibits higher seismic velocities than the surrounding mantle at depths of 150 to 250 km, resulting in high-velocity anomalies rather than the previously assumed low-velocity anomalies. Furthermore, the seismic velocity difference between hydrous and dry oceanic crust is less than 2%, making it challenging to distinguish between them using seismic velocities. This limitation may hinder the detection of the hydration state in subducted crust. In addition, lawsonite remains stable in 90% of subduction zones, and thus, such “seismically invisible water” may exist in most subducted slabs around the world.

title: 3D Outcrop-Based Carbonate Seismic Property Model: A Medium to Model the Impact of Meter-Scale Near-Surface Geological Heterogeneity on Seismic Data
abstract: The published dataset is a high-resolution 3D seismic property model. The model explicitly captures meter-scale facies heterogeneity representing the typical near-surface geology of desert carbonate strata. The model is provided in 32-bit SEG-Y format, ready for direct use in seismic modeling and simulation software. The model dimensions are ~4 km x 4 km x 155 deep, with a fine grid resolution of 3 m x 3 m x 0.3 m (X,Y,Z).The model includes VP (m/s), VS (m/s), and density (g/cc). The model is constructed based on extensive Late Jurassic outcrop and near-surface core data. This model accurately replicates complex facies architecture and petrophysical variations observed in the shallow subsurface of the Arabian Desert. This resource is essential for forward modeling studies and testing advanced acquisition/processing methods designed to mitigate seismic data degradation caused by strong wavefield scattering from shallow geological heterogeneities.

title: Magma Dynamics and Cooling in Sub-volcanic intrusions: Insights on eruption potential from Finite Element Modeling
abstract: <title>Abstract</title> The emplacement of high-viscosity magma at shallow crustal levels involves a risk for volcanic eruptions but may also produce accessible heat sources for geothermal exploration. Assessing the volcanic risk and the geothermal potential of newly forming and existing sub-volcanic intrusions requires an understanding of their growth and subsequent cooling dynamics. Unfortunately, these processes cannot be directly observed in nature, instead modelling can deliver useful insights. Here, we present a series of axisymmetric Finite Element Method (FEM) models that simulate the dynamics of magma movement and cooling during the formation of a shallow cryptodome inflating from a sill. The melt and solid fraction and temperature-dependent physical properties of the crystallizing magma are determined by simulations conducted with the Rhyolite-MELTS code. The results of the FEM models allow us to investigate the role of magma influx rate on the fluid dynamics and magma cooling inside the intrusion during and after magma influx. We conclude that magma inflow dynamics governs the volume and distribution of eruptible magma, as well as the duration for which the magma remains sufficiently hot to either be remobilised for an eruption or used as heat source for geothermal energy production. These results advance our understanding of the hidden processes that occur in growing and cooling subvolcanic intrusions in nature.

title: Analytical methods for zircon U-Pb geochronology and Lu-Hf isotopes used to analyze magmatic and detrital zircon from the Zimbabwe craton.
abstract: These datasets include the analytical methods for: 1) U-Pb geochronological data obtained in-situ using a mass spectrometer HR-ICP-MS (ThermoFinnigan Element2) coupled with a Teledyne Analyte Excite 193nm excimer laser and 2) Lu-Hf isotope data obtained in-situ using the ThermoFinnigan Neptune Plus MC-ICP-MS coupled to a Teledyne Analyte Excite 193nm excimer. The zircon U-Pb and Lu-Hf isotope data were obtained at the Radiogenic Isotope and Geochronology Laboratory (RIGL) at Washington State University.

abstract: These datasets include: 1) U-Pb geochronological data obtained in-situ using a mass spectrometer HR-ICP-MS (ThermoFinnigan Element2) coupled with a Teledyne Analyte Excite 193nm excimer laser, 2) Lu-Hf isotope data obtained in-situ using the ThermoFinnigan Neptune Plus MC-ICP-MS coupled to a Teledyne Analyte Excite 193nm excimer, 3) major and trace-element compositions of bulk-rock samples obtained through XRF and ICPMS, 4) trace element compositions of detrital zircon from modern sediments obtained in-situ using a mass spectrometer HR-ICP-MS (Element2). Bulk-rock chemistry was obtained at the Peter Hooper GeoAnalytical Lab at Washington State University.

THE NUNATAK CRYO-VAULT HYPOTHESIS: A Unified Geo-Biological Preservation Model Linking Pyramidal Nunatak Geometry, Subglacial Void Formation, and Long-Duration Biospecimen Stability in Antarctica
abstract: THE NUNATAK CRYO-VAULT HYPOTHESIS: A Unified Geo-Biological Preservation Model Linking Pyramidal Nunatak Geometry, Subglacial Void Formation, and Long-Duration Biospecimen Stability in Antarctica Author: Mark Anthony Brewer Affiliation: Immortal Tek / CollectiveOS Governance: QC $\rightarrow$ GATA $\rightarrow$ GATA PRIME Provenance: Proof Vault (WORM Certified) Date: 2026 Status: Draft for Peer Review / Restricted Distribution 1. Introduction 1.1 The Antarctic Paradox: Destruction vs. Preservation The Antarctic continent represents the most hostile terrestrial environment for biological continuity, yet paradoxically, it serves as the planetary cryosphere’s most effective archive. The conventional glaciological model depicts the Antarctic ice sheet as a dynamic, destructive mechanism—a continent-sized grinder where basal sliding, internal deformation, and isostatic pressure work in concert to pulverize underlying bedrock and obliterate surface features. In this "mechanism-first" view, the ice sheet is an agent of entropy, ensuring that biological material is sheared, oxidized, or crushed into unrecognizable detritus over glacial cycles. However, a growing body of anomalous data challenges this purely destructive paradigm. The discovery of subglacial hydrological systems, such as the Vostok-Sovetskaya lake district, revealed that liquid water and thermodynamic stability can persist beneath kilometers of ice for millions of years. Furthermore, radar sounding (RES) campaigns have identified "ghost mountains," such as the Gamburtsev Subglacial Mountains, which retain sharp, alpine relief despite eons of burial—a geomorphological impossibility under standard erosion models. These features suggest that the ice sheet does not act uniformly; rather, specific localized conditions create "pressure shadows" or regions of flow separation where the destructive energy of the glacier is nullified. This report introduces the Nunatak Cryo-Vault Hypothesis, a theoretical framework that integrates geomorphology, non-Newtonian fluid dynamics, and the "Constraint-First" physics of the Universal Intent Layer (UIL).1 We posit that preservation in Antarctica is not accidental but structural. It is the result of a predictable interaction between specific geological geometries—specifically, pyramidal or highly symmetric nunataks—and the rheology of the overriding ice sheet. When these geometric anomalies couple with localized geothermal flux, they generate stable internal voids—"Cryo-Vaults"—that function as natural stasis chambers. 1.2 The "Constraint-First" Theoretical Basis To understand the formation and stability of these vaults, this analysis moves beyond classical mechanics and adopts the ontology of the Universal Intent Layer (UIL). Standard physics observes the mechanism (how the ice flows); the UIL framework observes the constraint (why the flow organizes). As detailed in the Universal Intent Layer Hypothesis 1, complex systems often exhibit "Over-Precision" and "Coherent Drift"—signatures of a system governed by hidden constraints rather than random stochasticity. In particle physics, this is observed in the Muon $g-2$ anomaly, where particles drift coherently to satisfy a hidden field symmetry.1 In the context of Antarctic geophysics, we argue that Cryo-Vaults represent a macroscopic geological equivalent of this phenomenon. They are "Pre-Mechanism Patterns" 1—structures where the chaotic entropy of the ice sheet is locally suppressed by geometric and thermal constraints. The Nunatak Cryo-Vault Hypothesis asserts that specific nunataks act as "Stability Kernels." They do not merely resist the ice; they manipulate the stress field around them, creating laminar flow regimes and static cavities that protect the biological information contained within. This perspective aligns with the Emergent Linear Feedback Engine (ELFE) principles utilized in stabilizing complex financial vectors 1, applying the same mathematics of oscillation damping to thermodynamic variance. 1.3 Scope and Objectives This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the Cryo-Vault phenomenon, structured to serve as both a theoretical foundational document and an operational roadmap for field validation. The objectives are threefold: Theoretical Unification: To merge disparate datasets—nunatak geomorphology, subglacial thermodynamics, and extremophile biology—into a single predictive model using the Geometric Anomaly Index (GAI) and ELFE stability metrics. Predictive Modeling: To derive a probability function, $P_{bio}(x)$, capable of identifying high-value exploration targets using existing satellite altimetry and ground-penetrating radar data. Operational Validation: To define the robotics architecture (CollectiveOS) and ethical governance protocols (GATA PRIME) required to explore these sensitive sites without inducing ecological collapse or biological contamination. 2. Background: The Geophysics of Ice and Rock 2.1 The Dual Geological Provinces Antarctica is not a monolith; it is a continent of two distinct geological characters that dictate the probability of void formation. East Antarctica functions as a stable, ancient craton. Here, the crust is thick (up to 40 km), cool, and tectonically quiescent. The ice sheet is massive, often exceeding 4,000 meters in thickness. In this province, preservation relies on extreme tectonic stability and "accretion" mechanisms, similar to those observed in Lake Vostok, where lake water freezes onto the base of the ice sheet, trapping ancient particulates. West Antarctica, in contrast, is a rift-dominated system. The crust is thin, extended, and volcanically active. The West Antarctic Rift System (WARS) provides a high geothermal heat flux ($HF$), often exceeding $100 mW/m^2$.1 This thermal input is the primary driver for "active" void formation, creating meltwater lubricated cavities and steam-formed caverns. The Nunatak Cryo-Vault Hypothesis is most active at the interface of these zones (e.g., the Transantarctic Mountains) or within high-relief ranges like the Ellsworth Mountains, where the geometric "stressors" (the mountains) intersect with the thermal "activators" (geothermal flux). 2.2 Rheology of Ice Flow Around Obstacles Ice is a polycrystalline solid that behaves as a non-Newtonian fluid under stress. Its flow dynamics are governed by Glen's Flow Law, where strain rate is proportional to stress raised to a power (typically $n=3$). This non-linearity is critical to the formation of Cryo-Vaults. When an ice sheet encounters a rigid obstacle, such as a granite nunatak, the stress field bifurcates into three distinct zones: The Stoss (Upstream) Zone: High compressive stress acts on the windward face. Here, the pressure-melting point of ice is lowered, often creating a thin film of regelation water that lubricates the interface. The Shear (Flank) Zones: As ice accelerates around the obstacle, shear stress peaks. In standard topography, this leads to chaotic fracturing and the erosion of the nunatak flanks. However, if the nunatak possesses high planar symmetry (a high GAI score), the flow can become laminar, preserving the rock face. The Lee (Downstream) Zone: This is the critical zone for vault formation. As ice passes the peak, a zone of low pressure—a tensile shadow—forms. In high-velocity flows, or where the bedrock drops away sharply, the ice may detach from the bed, creating a subglacial cavity. Standard glaciology treats these cavities as transient features that close rapidly due to ice creep. However, the Cryo-Vault Hypothesis posits that specific geometries and thermal conditions can stabilize these cavities for geologic timescales. 3. The Geometric Anomaly Index (GAI) Central to the identification of Cryo-Vault candidates is the observation that not all peaks create voids. Irregular, chaotic peaks create turbulence and erratic stress fields. Symmetric, "over-precise" peaks create coherent flow separation and stable shadows. To quantify this relationship, we introduce the Geometric Anomaly Index (GAI). 3.1 Defining the GAI The GAI is a composite metric derived from satellite altimetry (ICESat-2), synthetic aperture radar (SAR), and photogrammetry. It quantifies the deviation of a natural feature from the expected entropy of random erosion. It is defined as: $$GAI = w_S S + w_U U + w_P P + w_E E$$ Where the weights $w$ sum to 1.0, and the components are defined as follows: 3.1.1 Facet Symmetry ($S$) This component measures the deviation of the nunatak’s face angles from a perfect subdivision of 360 degrees. A perfect square pyramid has 90-degree separation; a triangular pyramid has 120-degree. The Constraint Connection: High symmetry ($S \to 1$) implies a structured formation mechanism. In the UIL framework, this suggests "Pre-Mechanism Patterning" 1—where the geological uplift followed a crystallographic or stress-constraint logic rather than random erosion. The symmetry minimizes rotational torque on the ice flow, promoting stability. 3.1.2 Slope Uniformity ($U$) This measures the variance in mean slope angle across facets. Cryo-Vaults require uniform slopes to distribute ice shear evenly. If one face is steep and another shallow, the differential pressure creates rotational torque that can collapse a subglacial cavity. Uniformity ensures that the "pressure shadow" is symmetric and structurally sound. 3.1.3 Planarity Consistency ($P$) This is the Root Mean Square (RMS) deviation of the facet surface from a perfect geometric plane. title: Unlocking socio-economic value to local communities from mega development projects
abstract: This policy brief reflects on policies and practices that pertain to local communities surrounding development projects such as mega dam construction, urban expansion and mining activities in the Southern Africa development Community (SADC) countries, focusing on Zimbabwe and South Africa. The reflection is underpinned by the Zimbabwe government's Vision 2030, which is an ambitious and transformative agenda aimed at achieving an Empowered and Prosperous Upper Middle-Income Society by 2030. The vision can only be realized through the implementation of successive national development strategies.

title: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF THE EDUCATION SYSTEMS OF GERMANY AND UZBEKISTAN
abstract: This article provides a comparative analysis of the education systems of Germany and Uzbekistan, focusing on structure, governance, curriculum standards, vocational education, higher education, assessment practices, and recent reforms. The aim is to highlight similarities and differences between the two countries and to identify opportunities for mutual learning. The research is based on a qualitative review of educational policy documents, academic articles, and governmental reforms introduced in both countries over the past decade. The findings show that Germany’s dual education system, decentralization, and strong industry–education cooperation contribute significantly to workforce readiness, while Uzbekistan’s recent reforms emphasize modernization, digitalization, multilingual education, and international integration. The study concludes that both countries can benefit from exchanging best practices in vocational training, teacher preparation, and quality assurance.

title: HIFLD OPEN US County Boundaries
abstract: This dataset represents the primary legal divisions of U.S. states, commonly referred to as counties. In Louisiana these divisions are known as parishes; in Alaska, which has no counties, equivalent entities include organized boroughs, city and boroughs, municipalities, and census areas, delineated cooperatively by the State of Alaska and the Census Bureau. Several states include independent cities functioning as county equivalents. The Census Bureau also includes county-equivalent entities in U.S. territories such as municipios in Puerto Rico, districts and islands in American Samoa, municipalities in the Northern Mariana Islands, and islands in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The dataset provides consistent county-level geographic units for national data presentation.

title: European Values Survey 2018, Norwegian Part
abstract: The fifth wave of the European Values Survey was conducted in 2018 by Statistics Norway and commissioned by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) in Trondheim where Professor Anders Todal Jenssen was the contact person. The European Values Survey is an investigation of sociocultural and political change in Europe based on representative national surveys of peoples’ values and beliefs. The first, second, third and fourth waves of the survey were conducted in 1981, 1990, 1999 and 2008.

title: Fine-Scale Features of the Sun's Atmosphere: Spicules and Jets
abstract: We present an overview of fine-scale features in the Sun's atmosphere, with a focus on spicules and jets. We consider older and newer observations and theories for chromospheric spicules and coronal jets. We also consider the connection between these features and some other solar atmospheric phenomena. We then discuss the possibility that there is a continuum of jet-like features ranging from spicules to large-scale CME-producing eruptions, all driven by similar magnetic processes operating on differing corresponding size scales. Future observational and theoretical studies will help clarify further the nature of these solar events, and elucidate possible connections between them.

title: Publication Trends in Artificial Intelligence and Journalism
abstract: This study examines the publication trends, dominant research topics, and regional disparities in academic knowledge production on artificial intelligence (AI) in journalism. Using a scientometric approach, we analyze 269 Scopus-indexed articles published between 2017 and 2024. Methods include bibliometric analysis, topic modeling with CiteSpace, and co-authorship network analysis with VOSviewer. The findings reveal a sharp increase in AI-journalism research, with the majority of publications concentrated in North America and Western Europe. Thematic analysis identifies five key research clusters, including algorithmic governance, data-driven journalism, and AI-assisted newsroom decision-making. Despite the growing volume of publications, citation rates per article have declined, suggesting saturation in the field. The study highlights the structural imbalance in knowledge production, with minimal representation from Global South scholars. Future research should focus on interdisciplinary collaborations, the ethical implications of AI-driven journalism, and strategies for increasing academic inclusiveness in non-Western contexts.

title: Digitalization, pollution and innovative development of Ukrainian regions
abstract: Data on Digitalization, pollution and innovative development of Ukrainian regions were collected from open sources of the State Statistics Service of Ukraine. Relative indicators in the structure of general values were calculated. Data were collected and shown as of the pre-war period.

title: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF THE EDUCATION SYSTEMS OF GERMANY AND UZBEKISTAN
abstract: This article provides a comparative analysis of the education systems of Germany and Uzbekistan, focusing on structure, governance, curriculum standards, vocational education, higher education, assessment practices, and recent reforms. The aim is to highlight similarities and differences between the two countries and to identify opportunities for mutual learning. The research is based on a qualitative review of educational policy documents, academic articles, and governmental reforms introduced in both countries over the past decade. The findings show that Germany’s dual education system, decentralization, and strong industry–education cooperation contribute significantly to workforce readiness, while Uzbekistan’s recent reforms emphasize modernization, digitalization, multilingual education, and international integration. The study concludes that both countries can benefit from exchanging best practices in vocational training, teacher preparation, and quality assurance.

title: United Kingdom Construction Market Overview: Trends, Drivers, and Future Outlook (2024–2030)
abstract: The United Kingdom (UK) construction market was valued at USD 316.38 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 439.04 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 4.3% from 2025 to 2030. Market growth is fueled by large-scale infrastructure investments, urban housing demand, and green construction initiatives, supported by government programs such as the Levelling Up initiative and multi-year social infrastructure funding. Challenges include regulatory complexities, labor shortages, and an aging workforce. Adoption of digital technologies, including Building Information Modeling (BIM), AI, IoT, and cloud-based solutions, is enhancing efficiency, sustainability, and project management across the sector. This manuscript provides a comprehensive overview of market dynamics, key drivers, challenges, segmentation, and competitive landscape in the UK construction industry.

Norway Construction Industry Overview: Market Trends, Drivers, and Opportunities (2024–2030)
abstract: The Norway construction market, valued at USD 65.32 billion in 2024, is projected to reach USD 101.70 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 6.0% from 2025 to 2030. Market growth is primarily driven by rising investments in infrastructure, strong government support, and key projects such as the E39 Rogfast Tunnel and Oslo Airport expansion. Despite challenges stemming from regulatory complexities and prolonged permit acquisition processes, the increasing adoption of digital technologies—particularly Building Information Modeling (BIM), AI, IoT, and cloud-based solutions—is enhancing project efficiency, collaboration, and precision. This manuscript provides an overview of market dynamics, segmentations, regional trends, and the competitive landscape shaping the Norway construction sector

An innovation measurement framework for the South African cultural and creative industries
abstract: There is increased scrutiny on the directionality of innovation systems in advancing critical global sustainability and development objectives. Equally, innovation policy mixes require complimentary measurement agendas to track activity and outcomes and inform public investment decisions. South Africa has a clear innovation policy mix for its arts, culture and heritage (ACH) dispensation. However, innovation indicators are not yet integrated within the monitoring and evaluation framework of the ACH dispensation. In this paper, a directionality-sensitive innovation measurement framework for the cultural and creative industries (CCI) is proposed with indicator categories addressing a fuller variety of system actors than are typically assessed in innovation surveys. The framework was piloted in South Africa’s Western Cape Province and yielded several methodological insights and data. Key among these is the value of survey interviews for data enumeration that bridges respondent understanding of the concept of innovation, as well as combining object- and subject-based approaches to mitigate against measurement error. By adopting this framework, data comprising a richer cross-sectional view of innovation in the CCI can be compared and analysed, in-country and across countries, enabling several potential research and policy monitoring use cases.

title: National Travel Survey 2001, Long Journeys
abstract: This dataset is derived from the study "the National Travel Survey 2001". The survey was initiated because the parliament of Norway (Stortinget) decided to conduct a national travel survey every fourth year. Similar studies were conducted in 1984/85, 1991/92 and in 1997/98. This provides a basis for comparisons over time. The main objective of the National Travel Survey is to map the citizens travel activities and travel patterns. The studies will provide insight about the scope of peoples travels, where people travel, how they travel, which parts of the population that untertake dfifferent kinds of travels and variations in travel patterns depending on where people live. Data about the populations travel activity is of great importance for national and local transport planning. The results will be used as a basis for the development of transport models, prognoses, exposion calculation in trafic safety work, and in a number of investigation and research projects. The National Travel Surveys are also an important basis for evaluating results connected to surveys concerning particular means of transport or spesific grographical areas. This part covers long journeys.

title: Bridging space and theory: trends in Czech spatial archaeology in the 21st century
INTERPOL as a Field of Geopolitics: International Abuses, Influence Structures, and the Transformation of Control in the Era of the Sanctions Ecosystem 3.0
abstract: This report examines the transformation of INTERPOL from a neutral mechanism of international criminal cooperation into a strategic arena of geopolitical competition embedded in the emerging Sanctions Ecosystem 3.0. Drawing on ARGA Observatory’s analysis of CCF decisions, RPD compliance, political-economic dynamics in the CIS, Central Asia and Eastern Europe, and hundreds of empirical cases, the study documents how Red Notices, Diffusions and in absentia arrest warrants are increasingly weaponised by authoritarian and hybrid regimes to pursue political opponents, influence corporate conflicts, discipline elites, and reinforce transnational financial coercion. The report demonstrates how INTERPOL has become intertwined with AML/KYC systems, FIU signalling and sanctions rhetoric, leading banks and fintech institutions to treat notices as high-risk markers and impose automatic freezes. As geopolitical blocs compete for influence within the organisation, INTERPOL risks losing neutrality, overloading the CCF, and fragmenting global law-enforcement cooperation. The study outlines typologies of abuse, regional patterns, institutional risks and a set of reforms necessary to restore due-process safeguards and protect the integrity of the international policing architecture.

title: Modernization and Growth in the Czech Republic Construction Industry
abstract: The Czech Republic construction market, valued at USD 28.22 billion in 2024, is projected to reach USD 39.46 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 4.1% from 2025 to 2030. Market growth is primarily driven by large-scale infrastructure projects, increased public investments, and the adoption of digital technologies such as Building Information Modeling (BIM). Key projects including the Wenceslas Square redevelopment, Metro Line D, Masaryk Rail Station, and Prague Ring Road are transforming the nation’s urban and transport infrastructure. Government initiatives, supported by European Investment Bank funding, aim to enhance energy sustainability, urban connectivity, and economic resilience. The integration of digital tools and sustainable construction practices is enabling improved efficiency, project coordination, and lifecycle management, positioning the Czech Republic as a growing hub for modern construction. This manuscript provides an overview of market dynamics, segmentation, regional trends, regulatory challenges, digital adoption, and the competitive landscape

Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data associated to publication "Kinematics of Burial Remagnetizations in fold-and-thrust belts: a case study from the South Pyrenean foreland basin (NE Spain)", JGR - Solid Earth
abstract: This dataset contains raw paleomagnetic demagnetization data acquired through thermal (TH) and alternating field (AF) treatment of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM), as well as three-axis IRM demagnetization experiments. Data are provided in the original export formats from the instruments used (*.dat, *.th, *.af), and in *rs3 format, which is fully compatible with the Remasoft software. The rs3 files include the interpreted paleomagnetic components used in the associated publication. Component C3 corresponds to the remagnetization identified as C3 in the manuscript, whereas component C34 corresponds to the published C4 component. These data support the analyses and interpretations presented in the related publication.

title: THE IMPACT OF E-COMMERCE AND DIGITAL MARKETS ON EUROPEAN ECONOMIC GROWTH: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF GERMANY AND THE CZECH REPUBLIC
abstract: .This article investigates the relationships between e-commerce, digital markets, and economic growth in the European Union, focusing on a comparative analysis of Germany (Western Europe) and the Czech Republic(Eastern Europe) from 2015 to 2024. Utilizing Eurostat data and a comparative case study analysis, the study finds that the Czech Republic, representing an emergent Eastern European digital economy model, achieved a higher average GDP growth rate (2.2%) compared to Germany (0.78%),despite lower absolute digital maturity. The results suggest that institutional flexibility, stable e-commerce adoption, and an export-oriented focus can be key drivers of growth in the digital age, challenging traditional narratives of an East-West ”digital divide”. The article contributes to the digital economy literature by highlighting the divergent pathways of digital transformation within Europe

JSIM 2025: Crise, Resiliência e Valor Público — Uma Análise Integrada da Edição Especial de The Journal of Sustainable Institutional Management
abstract: A edição 2025 de The Journal of Sustainable Institutional Management (JSIM) apresenta uma análise abrangente sobre como instituições públicas e privadas enfrentam um contexto global marcado por crises de governança, pressões geopolíticas, tensões sociais e desafios de legitimidade. O documento sintetiza evidências empíricas e contribuições teóricas distribuídas em quatro eixos centrais: (i) conformidade simbólica e isomorfismo institucional, com destaque para casos como Vale e setor bancário brasileiro; (ii) integridade organizacional e criação de valor público, apoiada na estrutura teórica de Mark H. Moore e na análise dos desafios de integridade em municípios de Minas Gerais; (iii) resiliência em contextos de incerteza, exemplificada pela implementação do Pacto Ecológico Europeu na Ucrânia em meio à guerra e por políticas de inovação no Banco do Nordeste; e (iv) governança interna e sobrevivência institucional, evidenciada pelo contraste entre cooperativas resilientes e cooperativas em liquidação. O conjunto da edição oferece uma cartografia narrativa da crise institucional contemporânea, articulando mecanismos de integridade, governança, inovação e valor público como pilares fundamentais para reconstruir instituições éticas, responsáveis e adaptativas. O material sistematiza insights críticos e propõe um guia conceitual para pesquisadores, gestores públicos, profissionais de governança e formuladores de políticas comprometidos com a sustentabilidade e a resiliência institucional.

title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Global Research Trends on Microfinance and Women's Empowerment: Insights, Patterns and Future Directions
abstract: This study aims to perform an extensive bibliometric analysis of international research related to microfinance and women empowerment using a database of 700 peer-reviewed articles within the Scopus database. According to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), we systematically screened and analysed the data using the Biblioshiny interface of the Bibliometrix package which is based on R. In this study, performance analysis, keyword co-occurrence mapping, thematic development (or evolution), and network analysis were used to detect the intellectual scaffold, conceptual trends, and emerging research domains in the sphere. The results indicate a thematic evolution from early day concerns on access to credit and poverty reduction to current concerns and social-responsive policies such as digital financial inclusion, gender-responsive policies, and sustainable development. Thematic mapping demonstrates that although classic themes, such as microfinance institutions and financial inclusion, are still in the limelight, scholars are exploring newer fields, such as fintech empowerment, intersectionality, and impact assessment. Temporal reviews with respect to temporal trends show an interdisciplinary blend and a rising significance of ethical, technological, and policy concerns. The present research improves the literature by providing a structured overview of the knowledge base, highlighting research gaps, and suggesting future roles in empowering women through microfinance projects.

abstract: The North American Atlas data are standardized geospatial data. title: The Probabilistic Nucleus as a Manifold: A Geometric Perspective on Top-p Sampling and Model Uncertainty
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language generation, yet controlling their output and understanding their internal confidence remains a significant challenge. Top-p (nucleus) sampling is a widely adopted decoding strategy that mitigates the risks of text degeneration by sampling from a dynamically sized set of the most probable next tokens. While effective, the properties of this nucleus set are typically analyzed through simple metrics like its size or the entropy of the distribution over its members. This paper introduces a novel geometric framework for understanding the probabilistic nucleus. We propose conceptualizing the nucleus not as a discrete set of tokens, but as a continuous manifold embedded within the high-dimensional probability simplex of the model's vocabulary. This perspective allows us to apply tools from differential and information geometry to characterize the local decision space of the model. Specifically, we investigate geometric properties such as the intrinsic dimensionality, local curvature, and volume of the nucleus manifold. We hypothesize that these geometric measures provide a richer, more nuanced characterization of model uncertainty than traditional scalar metrics. For instance, a low-dimensional, highly curved manifold suggests high model confidence in a few semantically related options, whereas a high-dimensional, flat manifold indicates significant uncertainty and a wider range of possibilities. Through a series of experiments on a pre-trained language model, we demonstrate that these geometric properties correlate strongly with generation quality and can predict model failures. Our work provides a new theoretical lens for analyzing decoding strategies and offers a promising direction for developing more sophisticated, uncertainty-aware text generation algorithms.

title: The Essence of Emergent Origins B: Verification of Non-Abelian Topological Order Emergence Based on Three Criteria
abstract: This paper systematically verifies the emergence of SU(2)1 non-Abelian topological order through three computable criteria: structural stability, information efficiency, and dynamical accessibility. In non-Abelian systems, the traditional topological degeneracy is insufficient to describe information compression efficiency; the quantum dimension must be introduced as the core physical quantity. Numerical calculations show that for system sizes L ≥ 4, all criteria exceed the threshold (> 0.5), confirming the robustness of non-Abelian topological order. The research further extends the criteria framework to models such as Fibonacci and SU(2)2, revealing the universal role of quantum dimension in topological information encoding, thereby providing a quantitative theoretical tool for evaluating non-Abelian topological orders and selecting topological quantum computing platforms.

title: Meta-Gating: Evolving Recurrent Architectures for Adaptive Sequence Understanding
abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been instrumental in processing sequential data, with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) architectures demonstrating remarkable success through their fixed gating mechanisms. However, the static nature of these gates presents a fundamental limitation: their inability to dynamically adapt to the varying statistical properties and complexities inherent in diverse sequential contexts. This paper introduces Meta-Gating, a novel framework for evolving recurrent architectures that enables adaptive sequence understanding. Meta-Gating leverages a meta-controller to dynamically learn and adjust the gating operations within recurrent units, tailoring them specifically to the input sequence's characteristics and the task at hand. By treating the gating architecture itself as a learnable component, Meta-Gating moves beyond hand-crafted or fixed gate designs, allowing for the discovery of optimal recurrent structures that are context-sensitive. We propose a meta-learning approach where the meta-controller, trained on a distribution of sequence understanding tasks, guides the evolution of recurrent unit gates. Experimental results across various sequential tasks, including natural language processing and time-series prediction, demonstrate that Meta-Gating significantly outperforms traditional static RNNs, LSTMs, and GRUs by exhibiting enhanced adaptability, improved generalization, and superior performance, particularly in scenarios requiring fine-grained contextual modulation of information flow. This work paves the way for more flexible and powerful recurrent models capable of truly adaptive sequence understanding.

title: Hybrid Real-Complex Linear Attention: A Mathematical Framework for Sub-Quadratic Transformer Architectures
abstract: The quadratic computational complexity O(N²) of the self-attention mechanism in Transformer architectures presents a fundamental bottleneck for processing long sequences. This paper introduces a novel Hybrid Real-Complex Linear Attention (HRC-LA) architecture that reduces this complexity to O(N) while preserving model expressiveness. Our approach maintains multi-head projection matrices in real number space (ℝ) for hardware efficiency while modeling the softmax normalization mechanism in complex number space (ℂ) using Random Fourier Features (RFF). We derive the complete mathematical framework for this hybrid architecture, proving that the softmax kernel can be linearized through complex-valued feature maps φ: ℝ → ℂ based on Euler's formula. The key insight is exploiting matrix multiplication associativity to compute the Key-Value association matrix S = K̃ᴴV in O(N) rather than the full N×N attention matrix. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that this formulation achieves a speedup factor of N/M (where M is the feature dimension), yielding approximately 40× improvement for N=10,000 sequences. We further analyze numerical stability properties, gradient flow through Wirtinger calculus, and discuss implications for signal processing applications where phase information is critical.

title: UHF/SZTM Substrate Communication Protocol (SCP) provides a mathematically grounded framework for phase‑encoded information transfer within a harmonic spacetime substrate.
abstract: UHF/SZTM Substrate Communication Protocol (SCP) provides a mathematically grounded framework for phase‑encoded information transfer within a harmonic spacetime substrate. Building on the Unified Harmonic Framework (UHF) and Stieve Zero‑Point Topological Mathematica (SZTM), this protocol formalizes how quantum‑level fluctuations, curvature modulation, and harmonic resonance can be harnessed to encode, transmit, and decode information across a spacetime manifold. By defining explicit mappings for phase deviations, quantifying bandwidth under curvature constraints, and modeling noise—including quantum fluctuations—the SCP demonstrates the theoretical feasibility of communication channels embedded directly in the substrate of spacetime. The framework integrates entropy‑information diagnostics, resonance stability metrics, and harmonic manifold simulations to provide a reproducible, computationally tractable approach to advanced substrate-level signaling

LOGORHYTHMIC TRAINING FOR CHILDREN WITH SPEECH DISORDERS
abstract: This thesis examines the role, structure, and pedagogical value of logorhythmic exercises in the correction and development of speech in children with speech disorders. Integrating movement, rhythm, and speech stimulation, logorhythmics acts as a multisensory intervention that strengthens phonation, breathing, articulation, and prosodic components of speech. The study highlights the theoretical foundations, methodological principles, and practical recommendations for implementing logorhythmic sessions in special education.

title: CORRECTIVE INTERVENTIONS FOR CHILDREN WITH SPEECH DISORDERS
abstract: This thesis explores the theoretical foundations, etiological factors, psycholinguistic mechanisms, and corrective approaches used in working with children who have speech disorders. Speech disorders—including phonetic and phonological impairments, expressive and receptive language delays, fluency disorders, and voice problems—require specialized intervention grounded in developmental linguistics, neurolinguistics, and special education. The paper analyzes correctional strategies such as articulation therapy, phonemic awareness development, multisensory stimulation, and language-enrichment techniques.

abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations are a common symptom of psychotic disorders, especially schizophrenia, but can also occur in other mental and neurological conditions. Comprehensive clinical assessment is necessary to determine their relevance to psychosis.

title: How does the perception of internal versus external voices influence the diagnosis of auditory hallucinations?
abstract: Perceptions of internal versus external voices influence the experience and diagnosis of auditory hallucinations, with cognitive and perceptual factors both playing key roles.

title: EFFECT ON VISUAL THERAPY ON BADMINTON PLAYERS: INFLUENCE OF PHYSICAL AND PHYSIOLOGICAL VARIABLES AMONG COLLEGE STUDENTS
abstract: Badminton is a high-speed racquet sport that requires acute visual-motor coordination, physical fitness, and physiological efficiency. While traditional training primarily focuses on physical conditioning and technical skill development, emerging research highlights the importance of visual therapy in enhancing sports performance. This article investigates the effect of visual therapy on badminton players among college students and examines how physical and physiological variables influence its effectiveness. Sixty students were selected from SDAT, Anna Stadium, Tiruchirappalli, ranging in age from 18 to 24 years. The participants were divided into two independent groups: thirty students in the experimental group and thirty in the control group. Data were collected through pre- and post-tests. The variables in the present study include physical variables such as agility, reaction time, flexibility, and speed, and physiological variables such as VO₂ max, resting heart rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure. The findings suggest that visual therapy can significantly improve performance indicators such as reaction time, hand-eye coordination, and spatial awareness, with variations in outcomes influenced by the athletes' physical and physiological profiles.

title: Determining the State of Jupiter’s Magnetosphere Using In Situ and Remote Sensing Observations
abstract: Abstract While Jupiter’s magnetosphere is primarily governed by internal processes, variations in solar wind conditions can significantly modulate magnetospheric energy. Assessing solar wind conditions at Jupiter has been a long-standing challenge in the community. In this study, we investigate multiple datasets, including auroral images captured by the Hubble Space Telescope and in situ measurements obtained by the Juno spacecraft, to characterize Jupiter’s magnetosphere during solar wind compression and quiet conditions. The distinct responses demonstrate that auroral morphologies, lobe magnetic fields, ultra-low-frequency waves, and broadband kilometric radio emissions could serve as effective indicators for magnetospheric states. In particular, we statistically analyze the distribution of lobe magnetic fields, which represent the intensities of the cross-field electrical currents in the magnetodisc, and propose the applicability of the lobe magnetic field as a proxy for solar wind conditions. The results from the four individual methods of determining magnetospheric states are generally consistent, providing further evidence of their robustness. These observational proxies for solar wind conditions could therefore be widely applied in both existing spacecraft datasets and those from future missions to Jupiter.

abstract: This thesis explores the theoretical foundations, etiological factors, psycholinguistic mechanisms, and corrective approaches used in working with children who have speech disorders. Speech disorders—including phonetic and phonological impairments, expressive and receptive language delays, fluency disorders, and voice problems—require specialized intervention grounded in developmental linguistics, neurolinguistics, and special education. The paper analyzes correctional strategies such as articulation therapy, phonemic awareness development, multisensory stimulation, and language-enrichment techniques.

title: Modality-Specific and Multimodal ‘Associative’ Forms of Face and Voice Recognition Disorders in Patients with Right Anterior Temporal Lesions: A Review of Single-Case Studies
abstract: Introduction: ‘Associative prosopagnosia’ and ‘associative phonagnosia’ are high-level post-perceptual face and voice recognition defects due to right anterior temporal lesions, but the relations between these two disorders are uncertain. It is, indeed, not clear if face and voice recognition disorders observed in these patients must be considered as independent modality-specific recognition defects or as fragments of a more general semantic disorder concerning the multimodal representation of known persons. Aims of this study: In this review, the relations between associative forms of face and voice recognition disorders were investigated in all patients with right anterior temporal lesions reported in the literature. A prevalence of ‘pure’ (modality-specific) forms could indicate that these are independent, modality-specific recognition defects, whereas a high frequency of voice- and face-associated disorders could suggest that they are components of a multimodal semantic disruption. Results: Results show that ‘associative prosopagnosia’ and ‘associative phonagnosia’ are observed sometimes as ‘pure’ forms, other times as associations between verbal and non-verbal defects of person recognition, and still other times as associations restricted to the non-verbal (face and voice) modalities of person recognition. Furthermore, in a patient with a multimodal face and voice recognition disorder, the lesion involved the right temporal pole, considered as the locus of convergence of face and voice recognition modalities. Discussion: These data suggest that specific lesions of the right anterior temporal lobes can disrupt the highest modality-specific levels of face and voice representations, whereas other equally selective lesions can disrupt the locus of convergence of face and voice recognition modalities.

title: Acoustic analysis of bottlenose dolphin vocalizations for behavioral classification in controlled settings
abstract: Understanding how bottlenose dolphins adjust their vocal behavior in response to daily routines can provide insights into social communication and welfare assessment in managed care environments. This study presents a detailed analysis of bottlenose dolphin ( Tursiops truncatus ) vocal behavior in relation to different daily activities within a controlled environment at Oltremare Marine Park (Riccione, Italy). 24 hours of continuous acoustic recordings were collected from seven dolphins during a typical day at the marine park, including training, feeding, playing, and unstructured activities. Signals were analyzed to quantify the variations in type and number of vocalizations in relation to dolphin activity. 3,111 whistles were manually extracted and stored as both normalized audio files and high-resolution spectrograms. Additionally, an automated algorithm identified 1,277 pulsed vocalizations, classified into echolocation click trains, burst-pulse sounds, and feeding buzzes, using signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and inter-click interval criteria. Results revealed a significant increase in vocalization rates during structured activities compared to unstructured periods ( p < 0.001). This trend was consistently observed across all four vocalization types. Notably, play sessions elicited the highest rates of pulsed vocalizations ( p < 0.01), suggesting enhanced social and exploratory behaviors, i.e., interactions with conspecifics as well as curiosity-driven engagement with the environment. To test dataset reliability and usability, signal quality was analyzed by evaluating SNR. To support future research in marine mammal bioacoustics, behavioral ecology, and Artificial-Intelligence-based acoustic monitoring, the full annotated dataset was released as an open-access resource.
