Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Intrusion Detection Using Hybrid CNN-LSTM with cWGAN-GP Augmentation and Human-in-the-Loop Feedback
abstract: Intrusion detection systems (IDSs) must operate under severe class imbalance, evolving attack behavior, and the need for calibrated decisions that integrate smoothly with security operations. We propose a human-in-the-loop IDS that combines a convolutional neural network and a long short-term memory network (CNN–LSTM) classifier with a variational autoencoder (VAE)-seeded conditional Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP) augmentation and entropy-based abstention. Minority classes are reinforced offline via conditional generative adversarial (GAN) sampling, whereas high-entropy predictions are escalated for analysts and are incorporated into a curated retraining set. On CIC-IDS2017, the resulting framework delivered well-calibrated binary performance (ACC = 98.0%, DR = 96.6%, precision = 92.1%, F1 = 94.3%; baseline ECE ≈ 0.04, Brier ≈ 0.11) and substantially improved minority recall (e.g., Infiltration from 0% to >80%, Web Attack–XSS +25 pp, and DoS Slowhttptest +15 pp, for an overall +11 pp macro-recall gain). The deployed model remained lightweight (~42 MB, <10 ms per batch; ≈32 k flows/s on RTX-3050 Ti), and only approximately 1% of the flows were routed for human review. Extensive evaluation, including ROC/PR sweeps, reliability diagrams, cross-domain tests on CIC-IoT2023, and FGSM/PGD adversarial stress, highlights both the strengths and remaining limitations, notably residual errors on rare web attacks and limited IoT transfer. Overall, the framework provides a practical, calibrated, and extensible machine learning (ML) tier for modern IDS deployment and motivates future research on domain alignment and adversarial defense.

title: Causal Abstraction for Scalable and Robust Action Planning in Partially Observable Environments
abstract: Action planning in partially observable environments remains a significant challenge due to the computational complexity of maintaining beliefs and searching for optimal policies. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging causal abstraction to simplify the planning process, enhancing both scalability and robustness. We propose a framework that automatically identifies and exploits causal relationships within the environment to create abstract models, focusing on the most relevant state variables and actions. These abstract models are then used for planning, significantly reducing the state space and decision complexity. Furthermore, we develop a method for refining these abstractions based on performance feedback, enabling adaptation to changing environmental conditions and improving robustness against unforeseen events. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments in simulated domains, showcasing its ability to generate near-optimal plans with significantly reduced computational resources compared to traditional planning methods. The results highlight the potential of causal abstraction as a powerful tool for tackling complex planning problems in real-world scenarios.

title: Emergent Routing for Dynamic Expert Specialization in Scalable Mixture of Experts
abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) models represent a paradigm shift in scalable deep learning, enabling models with vast parameter counts to achieve high performance with reduced computational cost per inference. Traditional MoE architectures often rely on pre-defined or statically learned routing mechanisms and fixed expert specializations, which can limit their adaptability to diverse and evolving data distributions, leading to issues such as load imbalance and suboptimal resource utilization. This paper proposes a novel framework for "Emergent Routing for Dynamic Expert Specialization in Scalable Mixture of Experts." Inspired by principles of complex adaptive systems, our approach allows routing policies and expert functionalities to co-evolve and self-organize during training, without explicit pre-programming of expert domains. We introduce a feedback-driven routing mechanism that adaptively allocates computational budget to experts based on their real-time performance and emerging expertise. This dynamic allocation fosters an organic specialization process where experts naturally gravitate towards distinct data modalities or task components. We detail a methodology incorporating adaptive loss functions, meta-learning for router refinement, and an implicit expert capacity management system. Experimental evaluations on large-scale datasets demonstrate that emergent routing not only mitigates load imbalance and enhances computational efficiency but also leads to more robust and generalized expert specializations, significantly outperforming static MoE variants. The findings suggest a promising direction for developing highly adaptive and scalable AI systems that can learn to self-organize their internal computation and expertise.

title: Beyond Parameter Reduction: Unveiling Intrinsic Task Structures Through Efficient Fine-Tuning
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a critical technique for adapting large pre-trained models (PLMs) to downstream tasks, addressing the computational and storage challenges associated with full fine-tuning. While existing PEFT methods, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and adapter-based approaches, have demonstrated considerable success in reducing the number of trainable parameters, they often overlook the intrinsic task structures that can be leveraged for more efficient and effective adaptation. This paper delves into the realm of PEFT, moving beyond simple parameter reduction to uncover and exploit the inherent task-specific structures embedded within PLMs. We propose a novel framework that dynamically identifies and adapts to these structures during fine-tuning, leading to improved performance and generalization with minimal computational overhead. Our approach integrates structure-aware techniques, such as adaptive rank allocation and sparse factorization, with efficient optimization strategies to achieve superior results compared to existing PEFT methods. Through extensive experimentation on a variety of benchmark datasets and PLMs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in unveiling and leveraging intrinsic task structures for efficient fine-tuning, paving the way for more sustainable and scalable adaptation of large models.

title: Dynamic Graph Checkpointing: Unleashing Terabyte-Scale AI Model Training
abstract: The relentless pursuit of larger and more sophisticated Artificial Intelligence models, particularly in deep learning, has led to a significant increase in model parameters and intermediate activations, often reaching terabyte scales. Training these immense models presents formidable challenges, including prohibitive memory requirements, extensive training durations, and heightened vulnerability to system failures. Traditional checkpointing mechanisms, while crucial for fault tolerance and recovery, often incur substantial storage and I/O overheads, becoming bottlenecks themselves. This paper introduces Dynamic Graph Checkpointing (DGC), a novel approach that leverages the computational graph structure of AI models to intelligently and adaptively select optimal checkpointing points. DGC employs a cost-benefit analysis based on real-time resource availability and graph characteristics, differentiating between critical and recomputable states, to minimize both storage footprint and recomputation latency. By dynamically identifying and preserving only essential intermediate states within the dataflow graph, DGC significantly reduces memory consumption and I/O pressure, thereby enhancing the efficiency and resilience of training terabyte-scale AI models in distributed environments. Our proposed methodology outlines an adaptive strategy for optimizing checkpoint overheads, offering a pathway to mitigate current training barriers and accelerate the development of next-generation AI systems.

title: Neural Graph Construction for Adaptive ANN with Query-Time Guarantees
abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search is a fundamental problem in machine learning and data mining, critical for applications ranging from recommendation systems to computer vision. While many sophisticated ANN algorithms exist, they often struggle with dynamic datasets, heterogeneous query distributions, and the need for stringent query-time guarantees. This paper proposes a novel framework for Neural Graph Construction (NGC) specifically designed for adaptive ANN search, offering robust performance and predictable query-time guarantees. Our approach leverages deep learning to construct and optimize proximity graphs, where graph edges are learned to encode semantic relationships and facilitate efficient traversal. Unlike static graph construction methods, NGC dynamically adapts the graph structure in response to changes in data distribution or query patterns, employing a policy-gradient based reinforcement learning agent to learn optimal graph update strategies. A key innovation is the integration of a verifiable query-time budgeting mechanism, which allows the system to adjust search parameters on the fly to meet pre-defined latency constraints, even under varying load conditions. We demonstrate the efficacy of NGC through extensive experiments on high-dimensional datasets, showing superior performance in terms of recall-latency trade-offs and significantly improved adaptability compared to state-of-the-art ANN methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides theoretical insights into maintaining query-time guarantees without sacrificing search quality.

title: Adaptive and Semantic Checkpointing for Ultra-Scale Foundation Models
abstract: The training of ultra-scale foundation models, characterized by billions to trillions of parameters and extended training durations across vast distributed computing infrastructures, is inherently susceptible to a multitude of hardware and software failures. Traditional full-model checkpointing, while effective for fault tolerance, incurs prohibitive overheads in terms of storage, network bandwidth, and I/O operations, thereby significantly impeding overall training efficiency and increasing operational costs. This paper introduces a novel approach, Adaptive and Semantic Checkpointing, designed to mitigate these challenges by dynamically adjusting checkpointing strategies based on training progress and system state, while simultaneously reducing checkpoint size through the capture of semantically meaningful model representations. Our proposed methodology integrates an adaptive decision engine that intelligently determines the optimal frequency and granularity of checkpoints, leveraging insights from training dynamics such as loss plateaus, gradient variance, and anticipated system instabilities. Concurrently, the semantic component focuses on identifying and encoding critical model parameters or learned knowledge into compact representations, effectively distilling the essential state of the foundation model rather than saving raw, complete parameter tensors. This could involve techniques like parameter criticality assessment, sub-model distillation, or layer-wise semantic compression. We detail a comprehensive framework for implementing this adaptive and semantic system, outlining mechanisms for distributed coordination, intelligent recovery, and the associated benefits. Preliminary analysis suggests that this approach can yield substantial reductions in checkpointing overhead, significantly accelerate recovery times from failures, and enhance the overall resilience and efficiency of training ultra-scale foundation models without compromising final model quality. The proposed system represents a crucial step towards more robust and sustainable development of next-generation AI.

title: Dynamic Parameter Sharing: A Primal Mechanism for Scalable and Generalizable AI Systems
abstract: The quest for artificial general intelligence necessitates systems that are both scalable to vast amounts of data and diverse tasks, and highly generalizable to novel, unseen environments or tasks with minimal retraining. Current deep learning paradigms, while achieving remarkable success in narrow domains, often struggle with these two properties, leading to issues like catastrophic forgetting, inefficient resource utilization, and poor zero-shot or few-shot generalization. This paper introduces and rigorously explores Dynamic Parameter Sharing (DPS) as a primal mechanism to address these critical challenges. DPS proposes a paradigm shift from static, task-specific model architectures to flexible systems that dynamically allocate, adapt, and reuse subsets of a vast parameter pool based on the demands of the current input or task. We elaborate on a conceptual framework for DPS, detailing how a meta-controller or routing network can orchestrate the selection and composition of modular parameters. Through this dynamic process, DPS inherently fosters improved parameter efficiency, mitigates catastrophic interference, and enhances transfer learning capabilities, thereby paving the way for AI systems that exhibit superior scalability and generalizability across a broad spectrum of cognitive tasks. We discuss its theoretical underpinnings, potential architectural realizations, anticipated performance gains, and the transformative implications for the development of more adaptive and resource-efficient AI.

title: Beyond Bottlenecks: Adaptive Information Routing in Encoder-Decoder Architectures for Enhanced Sequence Modeling
abstract: Encoder-decoder architectures have become the cornerstone of sequence modeling tasks, demonstrating remarkable success in machine translation, speech recognition, and text summarization. However, the traditional encoder-decoder framework often suffers from information bottlenecks, particularly when dealing with long sequences. This bottleneck arises from the compression of the entire input sequence into a fixed-length vector, which can lead to the loss of crucial information and hinder the decoder's ability to accurately reconstruct the output sequence. This paper introduces a novel approach to address this limitation by proposing an adaptive information routing mechanism within the encoder-decoder architecture. Our method dynamically routes relevant information from the encoder to the decoder at each decoding step, allowing the decoder to selectively attend to the most pertinent parts of the input sequence. We achieve this through the integration of a routing network that learns to predict the optimal information flow based on the current decoding state and the encoder's hidden representations. This adaptive routing mechanism alleviates the information bottleneck, enabling the decoder to access a richer and more context-aware representation of the input sequence. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark sequence modeling tasks, including neural machine translation and abstractive text summarization. The experimental results demonstrate that our adaptive information routing mechanism significantly improves the performance of encoder-decoder models, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the learned routing patterns, revealing how the model dynamically adjusts the information flow based on the specific characteristics of the input sequence.

title: Bridging the Reality Gap: Adaptive Planning and Execution with Uncertainty-Aware Policies in Dynamic Environments
abstract: This paper addresses the critical challenge of deploying autonomous agents in real-world dynamic environments, where discrepancies between the agent's internal model and the actual environment, often referred to as the "reality gap," can severely degrade performance. We propose a novel framework for adaptive planning and execution that incorporates uncertainty-aware policies to mitigate the impact of this gap. Our approach leverages probabilistic models to represent environmental uncertainty, enabling the agent to generate robust plans that anticipate potential deviations from expected outcomes. Furthermore, we introduce a real-time adaptation mechanism that allows the agent to adjust its planned actions based on sensor feedback and updated uncertainty estimates. The efficacy of our framework is demonstrated through extensive simulations in complex, dynamic environments, showcasing significant improvements in task completion rates and overall robustness compared to traditional planning approaches. This research contributes to the development of more reliable and adaptable autonomous systems capable of operating effectively in the face of real-world uncertainties.

title: Federated Ensemble Distillation: Achieving Robust and Personalized AI Across Heterogeneous Data Silos
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training machine learning models on decentralized data, preserving data privacy and enabling collaborative learning across heterogeneous data silos. However, FL systems face several challenges, including statistical heterogeneity (non-IID data), communication bottlenecks, and the need for personalized models tailored to individual clients' needs. This paper introduces Federated Ensemble Distillation (FED), a novel framework designed to address these challenges. FED leverages the concept of ensemble learning within a federated setting, where each client trains multiple sub-models with diverse architectures and initialization. Knowledge distillation is then employed to transfer the collective knowledge of the ensemble to a single, compact global model. This approach enhances robustness against noisy and biased local datasets, facilitates personalization by allowing clients to fine-tune the global model with their local data, and reduces communication costs by distilling the knowledge into a smaller model. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of FED, demonstrating its convergence properties and generalization bounds. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, demonstrating that FED significantly outperforms existing federated learning algorithms in terms of accuracy, robustness, and personalization capabilities. The results highlight the potential of FED as a powerful tool for building robust and personalized AI systems in decentralized environments.

title: Federated Ensemble Learning: Convergence, Personalization, and Robustness Guarantees
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across decentralized devices while preserving data privacy. However, challenges such as statistical heterogeneity, communication bottlenecks, and vulnerability to adversarial attacks hinder its widespread adoption. This paper introduces a novel federated ensemble learning framework designed to address these challenges, offering convergence guarantees, personalization capabilities, and robustness against various threats. We leverage ensemble methods to improve model accuracy and stability in non-IID settings, while incorporating techniques to minimize communication costs and mitigate the impact of malicious clients. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating the convergence of our proposed algorithm and its resilience to data poisoning attacks. Empirical results on benchmark datasets showcase the effectiveness of our approach in achieving superior performance compared to existing federated learning algorithms, particularly in scenarios with significant data heterogeneity and adversarial presence. The results highlight the potential of federated ensemble learning as a promising paradigm for privacy-preserving and robust collaborative learning in diverse applications.

title: Adaptive Resource Allocation via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Load Balancing in AI Workloads
abstract: This paper explores the application of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to address the challenge of dynamic load balancing in AI workloads. Modern AI applications often involve complex computational tasks that require efficient resource allocation across distributed systems. Traditional load balancing techniques struggle to adapt to the rapidly changing demands and heterogeneous nature of these workloads. We propose a novel MARL framework where intelligent agents collaboratively learn to optimize resource allocation decisions in real-time. Each agent is responsible for managing a subset of resources and interacts with its environment to learn effective strategies for distributing tasks. We design a reward function that encourages efficient resource utilization, minimizes task completion times, and promotes fairness among agents. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed MARL approach significantly outperforms conventional load balancing algorithms in terms of overall system throughput, task latency, and resource utilization. We also analyze the emergent behavior of the agents and provide insights into the learned allocation strategies. The results highlight the potential of MARL for achieving dynamic and adaptive load balancing in complex AI-driven environments.

title: Neural Graph Construction for Adaptive ANN with Query-Time Guarantees
abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search is a fundamental problem in machine learning and data mining, critical for applications ranging from recommendation systems to computer vision. While many sophisticated ANN algorithms exist, they often struggle with dynamic datasets, heterogeneous query distributions, and the need for stringent query-time guarantees. This paper proposes a novel framework for Neural Graph Construction (NGC) specifically designed for adaptive ANN search, offering robust performance and predictable query-time guarantees. Our approach leverages deep learning to construct and optimize proximity graphs, where graph edges are learned to encode semantic relationships and facilitate efficient traversal. Unlike static graph construction methods, NGC dynamically adapts the graph structure in response to changes in data distribution or query patterns, employing a policy-gradient based reinforcement learning agent to learn optimal graph update strategies. A key innovation is the integration of a verifiable query-time budgeting mechanism, which allows the system to adjust search parameters on the fly to meet pre-defined latency constraints, even under varying load conditions. We demonstrate the efficacy of NGC through extensive experiments on high-dimensional datasets, showing superior performance in terms of recall-latency trade-offs and significantly improved adaptability compared to state-of-the-art ANN methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides theoretical insights into maintaining query-time guarantees without sacrificing search quality.

title: Autonomous Schema Generation: Dynamic Function Calling for Adaptive AI Tooling
abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly large language models (LLMs), has highlighted the critical need for seamless integration with external tools and services. Traditional methods of tool integration often rely on static, pre-defined schemas, which hinder adaptability and scalability in dynamic environments. This paper introduces a novel framework for autonomous schema generation, enabling AI systems to dynamically infer, create, and adapt schemas for external function calls. By leveraging advanced natural language processing and knowledge representation techniques, the proposed methodology allows AI agents to understand the capabilities of unseen or partially described tools and generate executable specifications (e.g., OpenAPI, JSON Schema) on the fly. This dynamic approach significantly enhances the versatility and robustness of AI tooling, moving beyond rigid API integrations to truly adaptive and self-configuring intelligent systems. The research details the architecture of such a system, including modules for intent recognition, schema extraction, representation, and a dynamic function calling orchestrator, complete with a feedback and refinement loop. Experimental results demonstrate that autonomous schema generation markedly improves the efficiency and accuracy of tool utilization in diverse, evolving environments, paving the way for more flexible and intelligent AI applications.

title: Global Acceleration and Digital Transformation in the Cloud Computing Market
abstract: The global Cloud Computing Market, valued at USD 573.99 billion in 2023, is projected to reach USD 1902.66 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 18.7% from 2024 to 2030. Cloud computing encompasses the delivery of scalable computing resources such as storage, databases, applications, and processing power over the internet with on-demand and pay-as-you-go pricing benefits. Its exponential growth is driven by increasing digital transformation initiatives, rising adoption of advanced technologies including AI, ML, IoT, and edge computing, as well as the expansion of mobile and internet infrastructure globally. Despite challenges such as cyber-attacks and data breaches, the integration of hybrid cloud architectures, edge processing, and domain-specific PaaS/SaaS offerings continues to unlock new opportunities. This manuscript provides a comprehensive assessment of market dynamics, technological trends, segmental insights, geographical patterns, and competitive strategies shaping the global cloud computing industry

title: CollectiveOS v4: A Forensic-Grade, Governed, Multi-Agent Operating System for Artificial Intelligence
abstract: CollectiveOS v4: A Forensic-Grade, Governed, Multi-Agent Operating System for Artificial Intelligence Draft v0.1 — December 2025 Executive Summary The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agentic workflows into critical enterprise and governmental infrastructure has precipitated a crisis of veracity. While current Generative AI architectures demonstrate remarkable capability in content synthesis and code generation, they suffer from a fundamental "determinism deficit." The stochastic nature of probabilistic models, combined with the opaque "black box" operation of neural networks, presents unacceptable risks regarding auditability, chain of custody, and operational reproducibility.1 As organizations move from chatbots to autonomous agents capable of executing transactions and modifying state, the absence of a forensic-grade governance layer has become the primary bottleneck to deployment. CollectiveOS v4 introduces a paradigm shift from chaotic, probabilistic generation to governed, deterministic architectures. It is a multi-agent operating system designed to produce verifiable, auditable, and reproducible AI outputs. Unlike traditional agent frameworks that prioritize autonomous speed and emergent behavior, CollectiveOS v4 prioritizes forensic integrity and constraint satisfaction. It achieves this through a novel "Proof Chain" architecture—a cryptographic ledger that binds agent intent, computational lineage, and governance policy into an immutable receipt for every micro-transaction within the system.3 This white paper details the technical specifications of CollectiveOS v4. It outlines the Multi-Agent Orchestration Layer (governed by specialized kernels such as Giles and Rabbit), the Governance Pipeline (QC, GATA, and PRIME protocols), and the Forensic Proof Vault. By enforcing "constraint-first" mathematical operators 3 and leveraging OpenTelemetry standards for deep system observability 4, CollectiveOS v4 ensures that autonomous agents operate within strictly defined safety boundaries, rendering AI labor transparent, legally defensible, and suitable for high-stakes environments. 1. The Epistemological Crisis of Synthetic Veracity 1.1 The Determinism Deficit in Probabilistic Systems Contemporary AI architectures, particularly those driving Agentic AI, operate on a probabilistic basis. When an autonomous agent is tasked with a complex objective—such as "optimize a global supply chain" or "summarize a confidential legal brief"—it executes a chain of reasoning that is inherently non-deterministic. A standard LLM operating at a non-zero temperature will produce different outputs for the same input across different execution runs. In a creative context, this variance is a feature; in a forensic or operational context, it is a critical failure mode.5 This "determinism deficit" creates a governance vacuum. In a standard deployment, an agent might hallucinate a fact, access an unauthorized database, or exhibit bias. Traditional logging captures the input prompt and the final text output but fails to capture the state transitions, decision logic, and governance checks that occurred between those two poles. This lack of intermediate visibility renders post-hoc analysis impossible. If an agent makes a catastrophic error, the organization has no forensic record to determine why the error occurred or to prove that due diligence was exercised. This state of "governance debt" forces organizations to limit AI deployment to low-stakes tasks, stifling innovation.1 1.2 The Forensic-Grade Standard To mitigate these risks and enable the deployment of autonomous agents in mission-critical domains, CollectiveOS v4 adopts a "Forensic-Grade" standard. This standard extends beyond simple "logging" to encompass a rigorous, cryptographically verifiable chain of custody for synthetic thought. The Four Pillars of Forensic AI: Immutable Lineage: Every action taken by an agent must generate a cryptographically verifiable receipt. This receipt links the action to a specific policy mandate, a specific user request, and a specific model version, creating an unbroken chain of causality.3 Computational Reproducibility: The system must be capable of replaying the exact sequence of agent interactions (spans) that led to an output. This ensures that any decision made by the AI can be audited and reproduced by human investigators or regulatory bodies.5 Policy-as-Code Enforcement: Governance cannot be a post-processing step applied after the fact. It must be a runtime constraint. Agents must be architecturally incapable of executing actions that violate the GATA (General Alignment & Threat Assessment) or PRIME protocols.3 Trace-to-Hash Linkage: System observability must be cryptographically bound to the data payload. The observational trace (what the system did) must contain the hash of the artifact (what the system made), preventing the decoupling of action from result.3 2. System Architecture: The Multi-Agent Kernel CollectiveOS v4 is not a monolithic model. It is a distributed, multi-agent operating system designed to mimic the specialization found in high-functioning human organizations. It utilizes a specialized suite of agents, each possessing distinct architectural roles, memory scopes, and permission sets. This separation of concerns ensures that no single agent possesses "God-mode" privileges, enforcing a system of checks and balances.3 2.1 The Orchestration Core: Giles Role: Strategy, Orchestration, & Planetary Balance Function: Giles serves as the primary interface for intent analysis and task decomposition. In the CollectiveOS architecture, Giles acts as the "Pre-frontal Cortex," responsible for high-level planning and executive function. Unlike a standard chatbot that reacts to the last user message, Giles maintains a persistent model of the "Planetary Balance"—synthesizing data from the Universal Intent Layer (UIL) to ensure that local actions do not destabilize the broader system.3 Giles does not execute tasks directly. Instead, Giles synthesizes the user's intent into a structured Strategy Object. This object defines the goals, constraints, and required resources for the task. Giles utilizes a Constraint-Weighted Update Rule to ensure strategic alignment: $$x_{t+1} = (1-\lambda)x_t + \lambda C(x_t)$$ Where $x_t$ represents the current strategic state, and $C(x_t)$ represents the constraint-compliant state derived from the system's core mandates. This mathematical operator ensures that Giles's strategy never drifts into incoherence but constantly converges toward the system's defined constraints, prioritizing stability over raw speed.3 2.2 The Execution Layer: Rabbit Role: Operations, Task Execution, & Tool Use Function: Rabbit is the tactical engine of CollectiveOS. Once Giles has defined the strategy, Rabbit decomposes the high-level plan into discrete, executable micro-tasks (rabbit_taskify). Rabbit operates on a tight "Action-Result" loop, interfacing with external tools, APIs, file systems, and databases. Rabbit is architecturally bound by strict Resource Limits and Scope Constraints. While Giles thinks in abstract strategy, Rabbit operates in concrete file paths, API endpoints, and shell commands. This separation prevents strategic errors from becoming operational disasters. Rabbit's activities are heavily instrumented; every tool invocation is logged as a distinct span in the forensic trace, detailing the exact arguments passed and the raw output received.3 2.3 The Security Layer: Cypher Role: Zero-Trust Security, Fact-Checking, & Anomaly Detection Function: Cypher operates as an adversarial node within the mesh. Its primary function (cypher_fact_check) is to audit the outputs of other agents before they are committed to the Proof Vault. Cypher employs a "refusal-first" architecture, assuming all generated content is potentially hallucinated or malicious until verified against the constraint field. Cypher's architecture allows it to interrupt the execution pipeline if a violation of the GATA protocol is detected.3 It acts as the internal regulator, applying cryptographic signatures to verified envelopes. In high-security modes, Cypher utilizes independent "Verifier LLMs"—smaller, specialized models trained solely on logic and fact-checking—to validate the outputs of the larger, more creative execution models, reducing the risk of collusive hallucinations.6 2.4 The Simulation Layer: AION Role: Temporal Simulation, Causal Modeling, & Forecasting Function: AION is the predictive engine. Before a complex or high-stakes action is committed, AION runs a causal simulation (aion_simulate) to forecast potential downstream effects. This is particularly critical for "dual-use" scenarios where an action might have unintended negative consequences, such as environmental feedback loops or information hazards. AION utilizes a Predictive Update Rule to model future states without incurring temporal instability: $$x_{t+1}^{\text{pred}} = x_t + \beta(x_t - x_{t-1})$$ Here, $\beta$ represents the prediction inertia (safe range 0–0.2), allowing AION to forecast short-horizon outcomes to validate safety compliance before execution. If AION's simulation predicts a constraint violation (e.g., a high probability of negative drift), the task is rejected and sent back to Giles for re-strategizing.3 2.5 The Narrative Layer: Muse Role: Human-Computer Interface, Narrative Synthesis, & Explanation Function: Muse is the final translation layer (muse_narrate). It takes the raw, structured data from Rabbit and the verified facts from Cypher and synthesizes them into coherent, human-readable outputs. Muse is constrained to never "invent" data; it is strictly a "lossless compressor" and "stylistic formatter" of the verified truth generated by the upstream agents. title: Adaptive Memory Orchestration for Resource-Efficient Foundation Models
abstract: The emergence of Foundation Models (FMs) has significantly advanced artificial intelligence, offering unparalleled generalization capabilities across diverse tasks. However, their immense scale and computational demands present substantial challenges, particularly concerning memory consumption in resource-constrained environments such as edge devices, mobile platforms, and even large-scale cloud deployments with dynamic workloads. This paper explores the critical need for adaptive memory orchestration strategies to enhance the resource efficiency of FMs without compromising their performance. We propose a comprehensive framework for adaptive memory orchestration that integrates various techniques, including dynamic layer-wise memory management, intelligent parameter fine-tuning, adaptive quantization, and efficient Key-Value (KV) cache handling. Drawing upon recent advancements in container-based orchestration, resource-efficient transfer learning, and specialized hardware architectures, this framework dynamically adjusts memory allocation and data flow based on real-time workload characteristics, model specifics, and available hardware resources. By synthesizing methodologies from adaptive inference, channel-adaptive self-supervised learning, and heterogeneous computing, our approach aims to minimize peak memory usage, reduce training and inference latency, and improve overall system throughput. The discussion highlights the potential for significant gains in energy efficiency and scalability, paving the way for wider deployment of sophisticated FMs in ecologically and economically sensitive applications.

title: The Scarcity Principle: Architecting Ultra-Efficient Deep Networks from First Principles
abstract: The relentless pursuit of higher accuracy in deep learning has led to an exponential increase in model size and computational demands, rendering many state-of-the-art networks impractical for resource-constrained environments or real-time applications. This paper introduces "The Scarcity Principle" as a foundational paradigm for architecting ultra-efficient deep networks. Moving beyond conventional post-hoc compression techniques, this principle advocates for designing neural networks with intrinsic sparsity and minimal resource footprint from their initial conception. We explore methodologies that embed scarcity directly into architectural choices, training algorithms, and regularization strategies, drawing inspiration from biological neural systems and recent theoretical advancements like the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis. By enforcing explicit constraints on parameter count, computational operations (FLOPs), and memory access patterns during the design phase, we demonstrate how networks can achieve comparable or superior performance to their dense counterparts while drastically reducing energy consumption and inference latency. The proposed framework integrates structured sparsity, dynamic pruning, and hardware-aware optimization to foster the development of truly efficient deep learning models. This work provides a comprehensive review of existing sparse training techniques and outlines a novel path for building the next generation of deep neural networks that are efficient by design, not by afterthought.

We propose a comprehensive framework for adaptive memory orchestration that integrates various techniques, including dynamic layer-wise memory management, intelligent parameter fine-tuning, adaptive quantization, and efficient Key-Value (KV) cache handling. Drawing upon recent advancements in container-based orchestration, resource-efficient transfer learning, and specialized hardware architectures, this framework dynamically adjusts memory allocation and data flow based on real-time workload characteristics, model specifics, and available hardware resources. By synthesizing methodologies from adaptive inference, channel-adaptive self-supervised learning, and heterogeneous computing, our approach aims to minimize peak memory usage, reduce training and inference latency, and improve overall system throughput. The discussion highlights the potential for significant gains in energy efficiency and scalability, paving the way for wider deployment of sophisticated FMs in ecologically and economically sensitive applications.

title: Beyond Data and Model Parallelism: Exploiting Hierarchical Concurrency for Scalable Deep Learning
abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various domains, but their computational demands continue to grow exponentially. Traditional data and model parallelism strategies often fall short in addressing the scalability challenges posed by these increasingly complex models and massive datasets. This paper explores hierarchical concurrency as a novel approach to unlock the full potential of parallel computing resources for deep learning. We propose a framework that combines data, model, and task parallelism in a hierarchical manner, enabling fine-grained exploitation of concurrency at different levels of the computational graph. We introduce algorithms for adaptive resource allocation and scheduling that dynamically adjust the degree of parallelism based on the characteristics of the model, data, and hardware. Furthermore, we present experimental results on large-scale deep learning benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements in training time and resource utilization compared to state-of-the-art data and model parallelism techniques. This hierarchical approach promises to accelerate the training of future deep learning models and enable new applications that were previously infeasible due to computational limitations.

title: Optimized Fault-Tolerant Data Processing Module for High-Reliability CNN Accelerator
abstract: Convolutional neural networks have become the foundation of image-inference tasks, with systolic array architectures providing enhanced computational performance and efficiency. However, the numerous processing elements (PEs) involved introduces significant challenges in terms of hardware overhead and reliability, which typically exhibit a trade-off relationship. Enhancing the efficiency and reliability of individual PEs can effectively address these challenges and substantially improve the overall performance of systolic array systems. We propose a module that can be implemented in PEs by integrating local binary patterns and min-max operations to reduce both power consumption and hardware size. This approach reutilizes the optimized architecture for fault detection, thus effectively minimizing the testing overhead. Our method enhances the overall system reliability by implementing a fault-PE bypass mechanism, thereby ensuring a robust operation. Experimental results show that the proposed module reduces the hardware area by 29.03% compared with previous circuits when synthesized with the Nan Gate 45 nm library. Furthermore, its dynamic power consumption is 13.72% lower compared with that of existing circuits when implemented on a field-programmable gate array. The results of a fault-injection experiment show that the proposed module reduces errors by up to 33.57% compared with previous circuits and that its test coverage exceeds 94%, with stuck-at 1 faults on PE input registers.

title: Beyond Amdahl's Law: Algorithmic Sparsity and Hardware-Aware Acceleration for Scalable AI
abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of Amdahl's Law in the context of modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads, which are characterized by massive parallelism and data dependency. We argue that algorithmic sparsity and hardware-aware acceleration techniques provide pathways to overcome these limitations and achieve scalable AI performance. Algorithmic sparsity, achieved through techniques such as pruning and quantization, reduces the computational and memory requirements of AI models. Hardware-aware acceleration, enabled by specialized architectures like GPUs, FPGAs, and ASICs, exploits the inherent parallelism in AI algorithms to deliver significant performance gains. We present a comprehensive analysis of these approaches, discussing their theoretical foundations, practical implementations, and trade-offs. Furthermore, we explore novel hardware-software co-design strategies that leverage algorithmic sparsity to optimize hardware utilization and energy efficiency. Our results demonstrate the potential of these techniques to significantly improve the scalability and performance of AI applications, paving the way for the development of more powerful and efficient AI systems.

title: The GPU-TPU Architecture Continuum: Unlocking Peta-Scale AI Efficiency
abstract: The relentless expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, particularly in deep learning, has spurred an unprecedented demand for computational power, pushing the boundaries from tera-scale to peta-scale operations. Traditional central processing unit (CPU) architectures are increasingly inadequate for these demanding workloads, necessitating the rise of specialized hardware accelerators. This paper explores the architectural continuum between Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), examining their distinct design philosophies, strengths, and optimal application domains. GPUs, with their highly parallel processing capabilities and flexibility, have been the workhorse of early AI development, offering general-purpose parallel computation. In contrast, TPUs are highly specialized Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) designed explicitly for efficient matrix multiplication and convolution operations, which are fundamental to neural networks, demonstrating superior power efficiency for specific, well-defined tasks. We delve into how these architectures can be strategically employed, either individually or in concert, to achieve unprecedented peta-scale AI efficiency, focusing on metrics such as computational throughput, energy consumption, and scalability. The conceptual framework elucidates the trade-offs between programmability, generality, and specialized performance across this spectrum, providing insights into optimizing hardware choices for diverse AI workloads, from large language models to complex scientific simulations. This analysis highlights the critical need for a nuanced understanding of accelerator capabilities to unlock the full potential of next-generation AI systems, proposing that future advancements lie in intelligent workload-to-hardware mapping and potentially hybrid architectural designs that leverage the best of both worlds.

title: Elementary Characteristics and Energy Transport in Physical Reservoir Computing
abstract: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) exploits the high-dimensional dynamics of physical systems to process information efficiently. In contrast to digital computation, where logic is explicitly programmed, PRC leverages the inherent energy redistribution and dissipation of dynamical systems to provide memory and nonlinearity. This paper develops a perspective on the elementary characteristics of physical reservoirs, emphasising energy transport as the unifying principle. We examine how the echo state property (ESP) emerges through dissipation, distinguishing reservoirs from mere input channels, and demonstrate how ESP provides the foundation for reproducibility, fading memory, and computational expressiveness. Following the development history of physics, we move from classical physics, including classical mechanics and electromagnetism, to quantum mechanics, for a brief overview of PRC across different physical branches. Classical mechanical systems are presented as canonical reservoirs, with mass–spring–damper models capturing the interplay between inertia, elasticity, and damping as a computational substrate. We then discuss optical reservoir computing, where nonlinearity and time-delay memory in photonic devices enable high-speed processing. Finally, we consider quantum mechanical systems, where the quantum dynamics and decoherence govern energy transport, offering new opportunities for parallel computation. Across these domains, we show that engineering reservoirs amounts to co-designing energy flows, dissipation, and expressiveness under thermodynamic constraints. This perspective positions energy transport and ESP as fundamental to understanding and designing PRC systems.

title: THE ANALYSIS, COMPARISON, AND SELECTION OF MOTORS AND MOTOR DRIVERS FOR THE MOTION SYSTEM DESIGN OF A FUSED FILAMENT FABRICATION (FFF) 3D PRINTER
abstract: This report presents the design and evaluation of the drive system for a 3D printer, with a focus on the motor and motor driver components of the 3D printer which is used in 3D printing also referred to as additive manufacturing. The drive system plays a critical role in the performance and precision of 3D printers. Stepper motors, specifically the NEMA 17 model, were selected for their accuracy and cost-effectiveness. To control these motors, A4988, DRV8825 and TMC series motor drivers were examined. The TMC drivers were found to offer superior noise reduction and smoother motion compared to the A4988. The report also detailed the design methodology/materials & method, literature review, and rationale for selecting motors and motor drivers, their integration into the printer’s control system, and the testing of motor performance parameters such as torque, speed, and noise, with a focus on future innovation. The findings emphasize the importance of choosing the right motor and driver for enhancing print quality and efficiency.

title: Chip testing data and Parity Matrices for NB-LDPC chip designed by Peking University
From Static to Dynamic: Complementary Roles of FSR and Piezoelectric Sensors in Wearable Gait and Pressure Monitoring
abstract: Objective: Plantar pressure abnormalities have a significant impact on mobility and quality of life. Real-time pressure monitoring is essential in clinical and rehabilitation settings for assessing patient progress and refining treatment protocols. Instrumental and particularly smart insoles offer a promising solution by collecting biomechanical data during daily activities. However, determining the optimal combination of sensor type, number, and placement remains a key challenge for ensuring accurate and reliable measurements. This study proposes a methodology for identifying the most appropriate sensor technology for wearable insoles, with a focus on data accuracy, system efficiency, and practical applicability. Additionally, it examines the correlation between sensor signals and material behavior during compression testing. Methods: Two insole prototypes underwent compression testing: one equipped with a Force Sensitive Resistor (FSR) sensor and one with a piezoelectric sensor, both positioned at the heel. Three trials per prototype assessed consistency and repeatability. Real-time data acquisition utilized a microcontroller system, and signals were processed using a sixth-order Butterworth low-pass filter with a 5 Hz cutoff frequency to reduce noise. Results: FSR sensors demonstrated stable static responses but saturated rapidly beyond 20 N, with performance degradation observed after repeated loading cycles. Piezoelectric sensors exhibited excellent dynamic sensitivity with sharp voltage peaks but proved unable to measure sustained static pressure. Conclusions: FSR sensors are well-suited for static postural assessment and continuous pressure monitoring, while piezoelectric sensors excel in dynamic gait analysis. This comparative framework establishes a foundation for developing future smart insole systems that deliver accurate, real-time rehabilitation monitoring.

Automatic Wheel chair by using Head Movement
abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of an automatic wheelchair controlled by head gestures, specifically targeting users with limited limb mobility. The system utilizes an ADXL345 accelerometer mounted on a wearable cap to capture real-time head tilt (pitch and roll) for directional control. The control signals are processed by an Arduino Nano microcontroller, which interfaces with a BLDC Hub Motor Controller to provide precise and efficient locomotion via two 12V batteries. For safety, an Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04) is integrated for real-time obstacle detection and a dedicated Emergency Button is included, which deactivates the entire system for a five-minute cool-down period. The system's operational status (e.g., speed, battery level, obstacle proximity) is transmitted via an IoT module (ESP32/Wi-Fi) to a cloud platform for remote monitoring and predictive maintenance. This design emphasizes low-latency control, energy efficiency, and user safety, positioning it as a practical, affordable, and robust solution for assistive mobility.

title: OPTIMIZED DESIGN OF ULTRA-FAST PIPELINE FIR FILTERS THROUGH CRITICAL PATH EVALUATION AND ENHANCEMENT
abstract: In digital signal processing, a FIR (finite impulse response) is a filter whose impulse response is of finite duration, and, thus, settles to zero in a finite amount of time. This is often compared to IIR filters, which potentially can respond infinitely, even with internal feedback. In this paper, a new hardware design of a high-speed FIR filter using fine-grained seamless pipelining technique is proposed. The proposed fullparallel pipeline FIR filter can give an output sample in a few gate delays by placing the pipeline registers across and in between the components. Specific pipelining strategies may then be devised at the level of the critical path analysis at the gate level depending on the throughput requirement. This project has two other designs in addition, allowing a different throughput rate and a corresponding area. The recommended FIR filters are designed for maximum throughput in trade-off between speed vs complexity. A model is used for sim software and xilinx for actual implementation

title: Development of a Low Cost 3D Printed Myoelectric Hand using EMG and ECG Signal Fusion
abstract: For amputees in underdeveloped nations, the high expenses and complexity of commercial upper-limb prosthetics continue to be major obstacle to accessibility. The design, development, and testing of an affordable, 3D printed bionic hand with a dual-sensor interface is presented in this study. This system incorporates Electrocardiography(ECG) as a secondary control modality for improved stability and mode switching, in the contrast to standard myoelectric systems that only use Electromyography (EMG) and are vulnerable to motion artifacts and false triggers. Autodesk Fusion 360 was used to design the mechanical structure, which was then made of polylactic acid (PLA) and has a tendon-driven actuation mechanism controlled by SG90 servo motors. Band-pass filtering and threshold-based algorithms are used by the control logic, which is implemented on an Arduino Uno, to handle biosignals in real time. The ECG signal successfully serves as a safety interlock, and experimental results show a system latency of about 190ms and a strong object grabbing capacity. The combination of multimodal biosignals with additive manufacturing can produce a dependable, accessible, and useful prosthetic solution, as evidence by the fact that the entire fabrication cost was kept under 10000 INR.

title: "Project X Modulator" Upgrade to the Dish Sentinel Network: Passive-to-Active Hybrid Enhancement Using Project X Modulator (Patent Pending)
abstract: This short communication completes the three-step Dish Sentinel Network (DSN) trilogy. Building on the passive meteorological sensing foundation (Swygert, 2025a) and the open-source passive UAP-detection extension (Swygert, 2025b), we announce Project X Modulator (patent pending) – a low-cost, drop-in hardware retrofit that transforms every existing consumer Ku-band satellite dish into a steered, coded, passive-to-active hybrid radar node.Project X Modulator delivers 18–22 dB coherent processing gain and 6–9 dB additional link margin, enabling 25–40 minute severe-weather lead times and unambiguous 180 km UAP tracks at <0.8° resolution using only repurposed, discarded dishes. Full technical details are reserved to pending patents; schematics and firmware will be released under CERN-OHL-S v2 upon grant.

title: Neuromorphic olfaction: event-based gas sensing systems
abstract: Gas detection is important in different domains like gas leakage monitoring, pollution control, disease diagnosis, and so on. To prevent health hazards, it is equally important to detect the gas concentration level rapidly. Out of different types of gas sensors, Metal oxide (MOx) sensors are extensively used for gas detection because of their portability, low cost, and high sensitivity for specific gases. However, how to efficiently sample and process the sensor data remains an open question. In a conventional electronic nose (e-nose) system with an array of MOx sensors of different sensitivity profiles for target gas detection, analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) of fixed sampling frequency are used to convert the sensor data into samples which are then fed to computers or microprocessors for further processing. Samples are generated at uniform intervals irrespective of the presence or absence of gas in the environment whenever the e-nose system is turned on which could lead to data explosion at the processing stage for bigger e-nose systems with many sensors. Our nervous system also samples and processes sensory information from the external world. However, the external stimulus signal is not sampled and transmitted uniformly but only when there is some significant variation in this signal to be communicated further. Therefore, only relevant samples are processed by the nervous system, accelerating our decision-making process. Also, the important stimulus features are encoded in the samples such that further processing is greatly simplified. Therefore, developing the event generation and feature encoding mechanisms inspired by those found in biological neural systems for conventional gas sensing systems could be one of the possible solutions to reduce the computational load on processing stages and accelerate the inference process. This thesis introduces an analog front-end for one MOx sensor which converts the MOx data into two discrete pulses generated from two separate pathways. The output of this frontend shares similarities with the spiking output of a mammalian olfactory bulb and one of the event-based vision sensors. The gas concentration is encoded in the time difference between these pulses similar to the odor concentration encoding in the output spikes emerging out of two distinct output channels of the olfactory bulb. We show that for a gas pulse injected in a constant airflow, the time difference between pulses decreases with increasing gas concentration, similar to the spike time difference between two output neurons in the olfactory bulb. The circuit design was further extended to the MOx sensor array and this sensor array front-end was tested in the same environment for gas identification and concentration estimation. The next part of the thesis explores MOx data recorded for artificial gas plumes deployed in a constant airflow and different features were analyzed for gas concentration encoding. The feature most robust to noise was chosen and the sensor array front-end circuit design proposed earlier was modified to encode this feature into analog spikes for gas concentration estimation. This new design was also tested for the single gas pulse environment and produced promising results.

title: Demand-Side Energy Management Using an Economical Smart Energy Meter
abstract: The authors present a cost-effective universal smart energy meter (USEM) that supports both Prepaid and postpaid options that support different tariff structures like time-of-use rates, block rate tariffs, or a combination of the two. The smart meter incorporates a potential transformer, a current transformer, and a microcontroller with an integrated communication module. The connection between the utility provider, smart meter, and consumer is established via unique identification numbers for each entity, using a cellular network. Additionally, the smart meter includes demand-side load management features, allowing for control of electrical loads and the provision of emergency power during shortages. The meter can be remotely configured and reconfigured through SMS, without the need for hardware changes. Furthermore, the system monitors energy usage, detects meter tampering, and identifies faults on the distribution side. A prototype has been developed, demonstrating the system's practicality, adaptability, and multifunctionality through experimental validation.

title: Shape-conformal porous frameworks for full coverage of neural organoids and high-resolution electrophysiology
abstract: This source code corresponds to the study “Shape-conformal porous frameworks for full coverage of neural organoids and high-resolution electrophysiology” to be published in Nature Biomedical Engineering. It describes the general workflow of processing the raw data of electrophysiology as recorded with 3D organoid interfaces. DataAnalysis.ipynb reads the recorded raw data from multiple channels, which is a series of potential data points as a function of time. It filters the raw data, detects the peaks, and catagorizes the peaks of each channels into clusters. It plots the waveform of each cluster of each channel, following which clusters with artifact-like waveforms will be removed. example_data.h5 contains raw potential data from two example channels. One demonstrates the typical results of signal, and the other shows the case of artifacts. t.h5 contains the corresponding time points of the example data. RemovingArtifacts.csv will be read by the main code to de-mark the artifact-like clusters.

A prototype has been developed, demonstrating the system's practicality, adaptability, and multifunctionality through experimental validation.

title: COGTD: China's first nationwide dataset of onshore oil and gas storage tanks based on high resolution remote sensing images
abstract: This dataset fills the shortage in China's oil and gas infrastructure data and provides necessary support for achieving “NDC 3.0” and “carbon peak and neutrality targets”. By combining multi-source data with AI driven detection methods, this dataset contains accurately detected onshore oil and gas storage tanks across China. And we used a bottom-up inventory compilation method to quantify the methane emissions related to oil and gas storage tanks in China, providing a high-resolution methane emission inventory. This dataset provides a transparent and verifiable data foundation, facilitates policy evaluation, and supports methane emission reduction efforts. It includes four files: • COGTD.zip: 76,635 oil and gas storage tanks (10 attributes: coordinates, geometric properties, shape, industry type, administrative geographic info) from GF satellite images. • OGT_CH4_1°×1°.nc: 1° gridded Bottom-Up methane emission inventory based on COGTD. • OGT_CH4_0.1°×0.1°.nc: 0.1° gridded Bottom-Up methane emission inventory based on COGTD. • OGT_CH4_100m×100m.nc: 100m gridded Bottom-Up methane emission inventory based on COGTD. • Each_Tank_Emission.zip: Individual emission data (annual/winter/summer) for 76,635 oil and gas tanks.

title: Research on Wellbore Temperature Field Based on New-Generation Microchip Logging Technology: A Case Study of Drilling Fluid Circulation
abstract: Significant thermal dynamics occur during both well construction and injection-production cycles in underground energy storage systems. Accurately determining the wellbore temperature distribution is crucial for optimizing drilling processes, enhancing energy storage efficiency, and evaluating reservoir thermal impacts. Existing measurement-while-drilling (MWD) temperature technologies are mostly limited to single-point measurements at the bottomhole, making it difficult to obtain a full wellbore temperature profile. This study proposes a novel microchip logging technology that achieves breakthroughs in power control and high-temperature resistance through optimized system architecture and workflow, with a maximum operating temperature of 160 °C and the ability to function continuously for 5 h under high-temperature conditions. Field tests successfully captured dynamic temperature data during the microchips’ circulation with the drilling fluid. The study established a temperature field model, applied the temperature measurement data to the model improvement, and analyzed the temperature evolution laws throughout the entire process, including bottomhole circulation, reaming operations, and microchip deployment. The model exhibits excellent consistency with the measured values, which is significantly higher than that of traditional models. The research indicates that this technology can be extended to temperature monitoring during cyclic injection and production processes in underground energy storage systems, supporting the design and operation of underground renewable energy storage (URES) systems.

SlideRule
abstract: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.

title: OML-vect: Enabling Automatic Compiler-Driven Vectorization of Transformers
abstract: This is the supporting artifact for the paper titled ”Enabling Automatic Compiler-Driven Vectorization of Transformers” as published in CGO 2026. It includes the source code for the proposed tool (oml-vect), along with scripts to compile and reproduce all experimental results presented in the paper. We provide a Docker image containing all necessary dependencies preinstalled, enabling straightforward setup and execution of the experiments. The setup supports running the experiments on an x86 host, and it also allows cross-compilation for RISC-V ISA, and it automatically transfers the statically linked RISC-V binaries to the host to be then copied to the RISC-V target via scp. The reported results were obtained on Intel Xeon an x86 64 Intel(R) Xeon(R) E5-2630 v4 CPU @ 2.20GHz and a Xilinx U55C FPGA emulating an Atrevido 423 RISC-V 64-bit core with a 512-bit vector unit

title: Unleashing GHOST: An LLM-Powered Framework for Automated Hardware Trojan Design
abstract: Traditionally, inserting realistic Hardware Trojans (HTs) in complex hardware systems has been a time-consuming manual process, requiring comprehensive knowledge of the design and navigating intricate Hardware Description Language (HDL) codebases. Machine Learning (ML)-based approaches have attempted to automate this process but often struggle with the need for extensive training data, learning time, and limited generalizability across diverse hardware design landscapes. This paper introduces GHOST, an automated tool that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for rapid generation and insertion of HT. The research encompasses both the development of the GHOST framework and a comprehensive evaluation of its effectiveness across three state-of-the-art LLMs-GPT-4, Gemini-1.5-Pro, and Llama-3-70B. According to our evaluations, GPT-4 demonstrates the best performance by successfully generating and inserting HTs in 88.9% of its attempts. This study also highlights the security risks posed by LLM-generated HTs, as 100% of successful GHOST-generated HTs that completed inference within the time limit evaded detection by a state-of-the-art ML-based HT detection tool. These results underscore the need for advanced detection and prevention mechanisms in hardware security to address the emerging threat of LLM-generated HTs.

title: Effect of injection parameters on compression ignition engines: A review of methyl ester oil applications
abstract: This comprehensive review examines biodiesel as a viable substitute for conventional diesel fuel in internal combustion engines, highlighting its environmental benefits such as reduced emissions. Despite these advantages, the review acknowledges technical challenges and environmental concerns. It discusses advancements in biodiesel production, especially the one-step transesterification process, and explores the efficiency and emissions profiles of various biodiesel blends in generator engines. The review analyzes the effects of injection timing (IT) and nozzle geometry on biodiesel spray characteristics, with a focus on diesel engines equipped with common rail direct injection systems. It investigates the influence of nozzle geometry, injection pressure, and bowl geometry on engine emissions and performance, emphasizing the role of IT and pressure in regulating engine behavior. While recognizing biodiesel’s potential as a renewable and biodegradable alternative, the review stresses the need for ongoing research to overcome technical limitations and address environmental concerns, aiming to fully realize biodiesel’s potential as a sustainable energy source.

title: Quantifying carbonate microstructure using classical segmentation pipelines for CCS and radioactive waste applications
abstract: Abstract. Digital-rock analysis can now simulate pore-scale flow and geomechanics with high fidelity, yet routine application is still limited by the cost of converting images into pixel-accurate pore masks. Some porosity measurements measure total porosity, but flow requires connected porosity. The need to distinguish between isolated and connected pores is clearly important. The question is why it is difficult to identify connected and unconnected pores. To tackle this, we present a fully labelled 2-D scanning-electron-microscope (SEM) image dataset of outcrop carbonates designed to separate isolated intragranular pores from the connected fracture–pore network. This distinction controls seal performance in carbon-capture and storage (CCS) and radioactive-waste repositories. Each of the 29 056 × 22 952 px images were partitioned into 100 tiles (2048 × 2048 px), annotated by polygon tracing. We then employ and benchmark eight unsupervised computer-vision algorithms: Morphological Gradient, Distance Transform, Local Contrast, Watershed, Global Threshold, Gabor Texture, Refined Morphology, and Edge-based methods. We contribute (i) an open carbonate SEM dataset with labels separating connected and isolated pores, (ii) an efficient polygon-based labelling workflow, and (iii) a quantitative comparison of eight classical pipelines plus a Hybrid voting ensemble. These resources shorten the path from raw images to pore-network predictions, and provide a foundation for future learning-based methods.

title: Dual-stage framework for corrosion prediction in oilfield conditions combining short-term data and long-term extrapolation
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a reliable predictive framework for estimating long-term corrosion behavior and service life of pipeline materials exposed to high-pressure CO2 rich oilfield environments. Traditional models often fail to capture the dual-phase nature of corrosion – initial rapid degradation followed by stabilization – leading to inaccurate lifetime predictions. By integrating short-term experimental data with long-term extrapolation using power-law and exponential decay models, the proposed dual-stage framework addresses this gap and supports safer, more cost-effective operations in the oil and gas industry. Design/methodology/approach The framework was applied to L80-1, P110 SS and 2205 DSS materials exposed to simulated oilfield environments with CO2 partial pressures of 0.5, 1.1 and 2.6 MPa. Corrosion rates were measured at 7, 14, 21 and 28 days, and fitted using power-law and exponential decay models to extrapolate long-term behavior. Model performance was evaluated using statistical metrics (R², root mean square error and mean absolute error), and service life was estimated based on cumulative material loss compared to critical wall-thickness thresholds. Findings The dual-stage framework effectively predicts corrosion behavior and service life. The power-law model captures early corrosion dynamics, while the exponential decay model excels at modeling long-term stabilization, especially for corrosion-resistant materials. Results closely matched experimental data, with 2205 DSS showing the longest projected service life, followed by P110 SS and L80-1. Originality/value This study presents a novel, validated approach that improves prediction accuracy by accounting for both corrosion phases. It aids in material selection and maintenance planning, offering practical value to researchers and oilfield operators.

A comprehensive model for assessing the impact of CO2 purity on the value chain of Carbon Capture, Transport, Utilization, and Storage
abstract: This Excel-based model is designed to evaluate the techno-economic feasibility of the CCUS value chain for both pure and impure CO2 streams. It integrates mass flow compositions and capital and operational expenditures from 11 different power and process industries that serve as CO2 emission sources. The tool also models CO2 transport by pipelines, allowing users to specify details such as pipeline size, length, and the number of booster stations. For the utilization of CO2 through EOR or geological storage, users can input reservoir fluid flow data and key economic indicators. The impurities analyzed in this study include N2, O2, NO2, SO2, H2S, CO, and H2O.

abstract: Liquefied Petroleum Gas Combustion General Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG or LP-gas) consists of propane, propylene, butane, and butylenes; the product used for domestic heating is composed primarily of propane. This gas, obtained mostly from gas wells (but also, to a lesser extent, as a refinery by-product) is stored as a liquid under moderate pressures. In addition, there are high-purity grades of LPG available for laboratory work and for use as aerosol propellants.
